#1482. Mauricio Pochettino's 'kill' team talk - when USA were already 3-0 up - convinces Man United fans he's right to replace Michael Carrick

Published: 09:23 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 09:57 EST, 10 November 2026

Excitement is already building among Man United fans at the prospect of Mauricio Pochettino taking charge, if Michael Carrick is sacked.

Carrick is taking training at Carrington today and his future is set to be decided on Wednesday when chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox meet with minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco.

If United choose to axe Carrick as expected, with the club in the relegation zone, USA boss Pochettino is the bookies' favourite to take the reins at Old Trafford and footage of a passionate team-talk has convinced some supporters that he would be the right appointment.

A fly-on-the-wall documentary series called Behind The Crest offered insight into the 54-year-old Argentine's management style and recorded his half-time rallying cry, with the USA 3-0 up in a game against Jamaica during the CONCACAF Nations League semi-finals in 2024.

Pochettino is seen building himself up into a frenzy, telling his players: 'Every single ball is the most important ball. We cannot play like we are winning 3-0.

'We need to go there and show the mentality. Take the next 45 minutes seriously. Take it like it is 0-0 and we need to win the game. That is the only way we're going to improve in our mentality.

🚨📹 WATCH: Mauricio Pochettino’s half-time team talk with his side already leading 3-0 after the first half!🗣️ “No, we don’t concede. We CANNOT concede. We need to go there and KILL and PLAY.”THAT MENTALITY! 👀🔥#MUFC pic.twitter.com/aXuiZn20i3

Mauricio Pochettino's passionate half-time speech to USA players (above) has convinced some Man United fans he would be the right man to take charge is Michael Carrick is sacked

'Be respectful with ourselves, first we need to respect ourselves. We cannot just go there and say to ourselves, "okay 3-0, no problem, they concede, we concede". We cannot concede! We have to go there and kill!

'If you are tired, we have players on the bench who can make a clear, clear impact and desperate to play. We have to press all together. When you're tired you can say, "coach, I can do no more".

'Enjoy being serious, we need to score the fourth, fifth, the sixth. That is the way we grow and respect the opponent.'

Despite the rousing speech, the USA went on to lose the second half but came out on top 4-2 in the match.

The footage has been widely shared on social media in conjunction with Pochettino's links to the Man United job and plenty of fans endorsed the idea of recruiting him, perhaps longing for a manager who can fire up the players in the mold of Sir Alex Ferguson's infamous hairdryer treatment.

One wrote: 'That intensity is what i want to see at United, 3-0 up at half and still no letting off.'

Another posted: 'He is right man for this moment!'. But others were more skeptical, with one capturing the sentiment of other naysayers, writing: 'Even if you hype him he is still gonna fail... if the same board keep of making decisions.'

Pochettino's work with the USA national side earned more plaudits at the World Cup on home soil, where they played excellent football before being dumped out by Belgium in the last-16.

And another of Pochettino's half-time speeches was viewed as a crucial turning point for his tenure in the USA.

With the team drawing 1-1 against Australia in 2025, Pochettino ranted: 'That is football! If we want to compete and we are 1-1 because we have the quality, we need to show more quality in the next 45 minutes. Play together. If you make a mistake, I don't care, but communicate and fight. They [Australia] come and they fight. When are we going to fix that? The team is dead. You need to talk!'

It was the first time Pochettino lost his rag and raised his voice at players since taking charge and midfielder Sebastian Berhalter said the message of the speech was: '"We're American. We don't take s***." Even though he's Argentinian, he has that mindset of, "Look, this is what we do. This is who we are. This is what America's about." Even from an outside perspective, he showed us Americans what we're about. He really drills that into us.'

The USA won the game 2-1 and the manager later reflected: 'This speech helped and was a great opportunity for the coach to explain to the players what to expect on the pitch. It was a tough conversation, but I think it was necessary.'

Perhaps that tough love is what Man United's dressing room now needs.

As reported by Daily Mail Sport late on Monday night, Carrick is nearing the sack during this November international break after presiding over a horrendous start to the campaign with the club in 18th and been given a stay of execution.

It’s understood that the Old Trafford hierarchy would want to inform Carrick of their decision face to face, so there may not be any confirmation from the club until Thursday.

Pochettino, pictured managing Southampton against Sir Alex Ferguson's Man United in 2014, could bring the intensity fans have missed since their legendary manager departed

The 45-year-old turned up for work at Carrington at 7.15am on Tuesday to oversee training with the players who are not away on international duty amid increasing uncertainty over his future.

United sources maintain that a final decision has yet to be made, with the club reluctant to engage in a running commentary over Carrick's position.

Former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Pochettino has a £7million release clause in his USA contract. However, it is yet to be determined the true value of prising Pochettino out as that figure doesn't include buying out his backroom staff.

It is also believed within Pochettino's deal that there is another clause which would allow him to leave his US role for particular high-profile jobs, such as at Old Trafford.

As of Tuesday morning, Betfair have him at 4/7 with out of work trio Eddie Howe (5/2), Julian Nagelsmann (5/1) and Didier Deschamps (15/2) the next favourites.

#1481. Manchester United’s attack may be their best form of defence this season

Is attack going to be Manchester United’s best form of defence this season?

There was plenty to like going forward, particularly once United had nudged their way in front after their second lucky break of what had hitherto looked like being a tricky afternoon.

Give this team a little space and they have the attacking players to inflict some serious damage, none more so than Bruno Fernandes who, just five days after collecting the PFA Players’ Player of the Year award, scored a hat-trick in what was another inspired performance.

Ipswich Town will testify to that after a sobering second half when it felt like United were going to score with every raid forward and, for a time, even threaten to equal the nine goals they scored against the promoted side at this ground 31 years ago.

In the returning Marcus Rashford, whom manager Michael Carrick likened to a “new signing”, Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo and, of course, Fernandes, United have an intriguing blend of attacking players. Throw in Kobbie Mainoo who, on another day, would have stolen the headlines with an imperious display in central midfield, and one thing United are not lacking for is creativity.

Their offensive problems tend to come when opponents sit in and ask to be broken down. Hull City, of course, proved as much last weekend when United looked desperately short of ideas in attack.

But you would probably bet on Carrick being more likely to find solutions to that particular conundrum than some of the defensive headaches that again reared their head here.

A week after that shock 2-0 defeat to Hull, United were given another scare when Ipswich took advantage of more meek defending to lead and could easily have scored more in that first half.

With a couple of days of the transfer window still remaining, it would feel remiss of United not to add a quality left-back before the deadline passes.

Those 15 minutes in the first half when Abdul Fatawu gave Luke Shaw a torrid time, not least in that moment he raced away from the United defender to cross for Leif Davis to score, should tell United’s hierarchy everything about the risks of not reinforcing in the position.

Ipswich STUN Old Trafford! Leif Davis does superbly to volley past Senne Lammens and give Gary O'Neil's side the lead 💥 pic.twitter.com/sJ0XNf8OiT

Defensive rebuilding is next summer’s big project but some things cannot wait and that is before we get to some of the issues in the other full-back position, which Ipswich also exploited. Fatawu aside, Daizen Maeda and Davis caused Diogo Dalot and Mbeumo problems down United’s right and the excellent Julio Enciso was a persistent nuisance until the game fell away from Ipswich.

For all the defensive concerns, though, United were exhilarating going forward, especially once they found themselves in front after benefiting from a curious ruling that dictated Harry Maguire’s “accidental” handball in the lead-up to the home team’s second goal was “not punishable” because he did not end up scoring.

In other words, had Maguire himself found the net and not seen his cross-cum-shot deflect in off the Ipswich defender Jacob Greaves, the goal would not have stood.

Harry Maguire's shot cannons in off Jacob Greaves and Manchester United are in front at Old Trafford after a VAR review! 💪 pic.twitter.com/hUdogDQX6k

United were brilliant from that point on. There had been flashes of the threat they hold in the opening 45 minutes but thereafter Ipswich just found themselves routinely bludgeoned and unable to escape the tailspin. As the rain poured down, the goals poured in. Gary O’Neil, the Ipswich manager, talked about a lack of “emotional discipline” but plenty of teams would have found United hard to contain in that moment.

Rashford was a threat on his first start for United for 626 days. Harness his talent in the right way and he will be an enormous asset. Cunha’s withdrawn role, with Fernandes and Mbeumo routinely racing in behind United’s false nine, caused Ipswich no end of problems. Amad Diallo and Mason Mount were missing through injury and Benjamin Sesko, a substitute, is still working his way back to fitness after missing all of pre-season. Patrick Dorgu almost scored a couple after coming on. So Carrick has plenty of options.

Fernandes was at his irrepressible best, initially punishing poor Marcelino Núñez after his slip allowed Cunha to play in the United captain to equalise five minutes before the restart and then taking the game away from Ipswich in the second.

Bruno Fernandes equalises for Manchester United! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/CdEI1REeUD

After missing two penalties in pre-season, he made no mistake from the spot after Greaves had brought down Cunha. He then steered home a close-range finish after Mbeumo’s shot was blocked and almost lobbed the Ipswich goalkeeper Kjell Scherpen from 60 yards. His last act was to send Mbeumo through to score with a delicious lob.

"He's the prince of this place!"Bruno Fernandes completes his hat-trick 🎩 pic.twitter.com/KgLlaMcKGR

This was the first time United had scored five goals in a Premier League game since beating Leeds United five years ago and you had to go back 10 years to find the last time they had more shots in a league match.

“There was a good mixture [in attack] there,” Carrick said. “Obviously we’ve got to find the right balance and options. We can play slightly different ways across the front line and a lot of the front players can play different roles.

“It was a little bit different today playing Cunha a bit deeper, and Bryan and Marcus a little bit higher. So it’s up to us to try and get that balance right, but certainly there’s creation and there’s goals within the squad, for sure.”

There was little doubt United benefited from the return of Mainoo in midfield. Summer signing Andrey Santos was the one to make way and Mainoo in turn produced the kind of intelligent, inventive display alongside Youri Tielemans that makes you wonder how Thomas Tuchel did not give the midfielder a minute for England at this summer’s World Cup.

He recycles possession beautifully, excels in the tight spaces, has a nose for goal and an eye for a pass and a lovely ability to glide past players even though he is not quick. Ipswich could not live with him.

Asked where Mainoo could still develop, Carrick said, half in jest: “On today’s performance, not much, really. I thought he was pretty much all-around, very, very good for a first start back. I understand Bruno will get a lot of credit today, and he deserves that as well, but I thought Kobbie was immense in the middle of the pitch for us and underpinned the performance of the team.”

The Man Utd head coach told Sky Sports: “It was a good win. It was a really good win in the end. We played some really good football. The biggest thing today was the mentality of the boys tp overcomes setbacks. We’re going to have them and it depends on how you deal with them. I was really pleased with that. It’s easy to look at the result but the mentality and the stubbornness really pleased me.

“We controlled the game pretty well for the most part. A lot of our play was looking on the way to how we wanted it to look. The boys took it on really well and we were fabulous.”

And on Bruno Fernandes, Carrick added: “He showed his quality today. Bruno did what he’s good at. He’s had a big week winning awards. Three goals and a fantastic performance.

“There were a lot of positives with and without the ball but it’s the whole mentality dealing with it and trusting each other. Last week didn’t go for us and we accept that. Today was a lot better.

“We’re not getting carried away. We were down last week but everything wasn’t wrong. We can still get better, we haven’t cracked it. We’ll get ready for the next.”

Speaking with Sky Sports, he said: “Really unlucky to be 2-1 down, really unlucky - two of the most unlucky goals you will see, but then not good enough to get back into it. We got punished by a very good side.

“To beat Manchester United at Old Trafford you need the moments to go in your favour and they didn’t. Rules can go against you, or a deflection, there are lots of things that can happen in a game that are beyond your control.

“It is a complicated rule - handball if it’s the goal scorer but not if it takes a deflection and was heading off the target. I think that is tough for a referee.

“But no problem. I’m not here to moan about refs. We get no points, at Old Trafford a lot of people leave with no points but we leave with an understanding of where to get better.

“We have three points from two tough games. A good start for us. It is the Premier League, the lads understand there will be highs and lows. We don’t want there to be too many lows but the lads are fine in there. They understand.”

"I understand the rules, but it doesn't feel right" Ashley Young and Darren Bent react to the reasoning behind Harry Maguire's potential handball not being given 🎙️ pic.twitter.com/MGJdBNhbYx

"We deserved that little bit of luck"Harry Maguire discusses Manchester United's controversial second goal where he appeared to handle the ball 🗣️ pic.twitter.com/AY3vWRCxZZ

The hat-trick hero told Sky Sports: “It was a massive result for us. We lost three points last week. First game at home, the fans have been waiting for this. It’s not to make up for last week, you can’t get six points from it. Second half we were very good.

“Scoring before half-time is always important if it’s to get on top of the game or draw the game. We were in control of the game. In the second half, we were very good.

“Scoring goals is the best feeling in football. Doing a half-time at home with our fans is something I’m proud of. I hope I can do much more and help my team-mate score goals too.”

Dorgu looks hungry for a goal as he fires a thunderbolt towards Scherpen’s near post. The Ipswich goalkeeper is up to the task and bats the shot away for a corner.

Man Utd are pushing for a sixth goal and come scarily close to it, but Dorgo’s close-range header is parried away by Scherpen.

Five-star Man Utd are ripping Ipswich apart again. He didn’t score it, but Fernandes is at the heart of this goal. The playmaker floats a delightful ball over Ipswich’s defence for Mbeumo to chase. Carrick orders a triple change as the rain begins to hammer down at Old Trafford. Cunha, Mainoo and Rashford depart for Sesko, Andrey Santos and Dorgu.

Man Utd are close to a fifth goal, but Cunha is denied by Scherpen at his near post. Just before that, Rashford showcased some exceptional skill and nutmegged Diop, but he couldn’t quite get a shot away.

After a flurry of changes for Ipswich amid the chaos, they’ve switched to a back five. Nunez, Lukic and Maeda are all off, with Palacios, Ouattara and Furlong on as the replacements. For Man Utd, Dalot and Shaw are withdrawn for Yoro and Mazraoui.

Fernandes is overflowing with confidence and attempts to lob Scherpen from near the half-way line. His cheeky attempt shaves the roof of the net.

Mbeumo’s blocked effort kindly falls into Fernandes’ path and once again, the Man Utd displays unerring compsure to calmly slide the ball into the bottom corner from close range, leaving Scherpen with no chance. Man Utd are in cruise control now.

Rashford meets a clipped cross, but on this occasion, Scherpen is there to make a strong save.

The Portuguese playmaker is the most composed man in Old Trafford. Fernandes coolly sends Scherpen the wrong way and Man Utd now have an invaluable two-goal advantage.

Bruno Fernandes makes it 3-1 to Manchester United from the spot 🎯 pic.twitter.com/vFh7moSSpb

Wave after wave of Man Utd pressure has finally paid off. Man Utd have Ipswich trapped inside their own half as Akpom attempts to chip the ball over Maguire, who blocks it. Ipswich have looked very useful going forward and richly deserved their opening goal. Fatawu’s dazzling run was rewarded by Davis’ composed finish, but the visitors’ lead didn’t last long. Nunez’s slip proved costly, with Cunha and Fernandes combining to devastating effect, hauling Man Utd level.

And United haven’t learned from it. Moments later and Fatawu clips in a cross - with not nearly enough pressure from Shaw to shut it out - and Davis is again unmarked at the back with Dalot occupied and Mbeumo ball watching. There’s an early roar from the Old Trafford crowd as Rashford gets on the ball and sprints at Ipswich captain O’Shea, who is playing at right back.

Against Hull, Man Utd’s forward line looked way off the pace. In an attempt to stop history repeating itself, Michael Carrick has turned to Marcus Rashford, who is making his first start for the club since the end of 2024.

When Rashford last featured for Man Utd, he was wearing the No.10 shirt. That is now occupied by Mathues Cunha who starts as the central frontman, with Rashford now sporting the No.9.

The hosts will also need captain Bruno Fernandes to deliver. He will levels below his exceptionally high standards last time out, while Bryan Mbeumo also needs to make more of an impact.

It was short and not sweet. Playing in their first top-flight campaign since 2001-02, Ipswich finished 19th with just 22 points under Kieran McKenna.

This time, Gary O’Neil is the boss and they’ve already ticked off one victory thanks to those three points against Sunderland.

Is he the man to guide Ipswich to safety?

There’s going to be an onus on Rashford and Bryan Mbeumo to provide pace and penetration from out wide and get in behind Ipswich’s defence.

Your Town at Old Trafford! ✊ pic.twitter.com/mVMj2LVNvs

Unsurprisingly, Michael Carrick has shuffled his pack after last weekend’s disastrous defeat to Hull. Rashford, Mainoo, Martinez and Dalot all come into the starting X1.

📍 Home.Back where we belong. https://t.co/VbvwRcdF4t pic.twitter.com/37rThnGjyN

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of Sunday’s late Premier League kick-off between Manchester United and Ipswich Town at Old Trafford.

Man Utd suffered an almighty upset last weekend as they slumped to a shock 2-0 defeat against Hull City in Yorkshire. The hosts scored twice after 38 minutes, leaving Michael Carrick’s men with a mountain to climb, but they simply had no answer so Man Utd were shambolic defensively and toothless in attack.

When the fixture list was released, everyone looked at Man Utd’s opening two games against newly-promoted sides as the ideal opportunity for maximum points. But now, there is serious pressure on today’s home team to deliver in front of their fans.

Reflecting on last week’s loss in a press conference ahead of this outing, Carrick said: “I think your success comes from how well you deal with setbacks in the end. In any position, or certainly any sport, particularly this one, going through a season, there are going to be setbacks, sometimes a bit smaller than others. It’s how you deal with that initially, how you react to it and what comes next. I think that ultimately decides what type of team you’re going to become.

“So far, we’ve dealt with those setbacks really well within games and game to game. We had one last week, there’s no getting away from it, and it’s disappointing, but we’re looking to bounce back. We’ve had a good week. The boys have re-focused, learnt from where we could have improved and kept pushing forward.”

Against the odds, Ipswich began their 2026-27 Premier League campaign with a 2-1 comeback victory over Sunderland, with summer signing Emersonn equalising before substitute Jack Clarke found a 90th-minute winner at Portman Road. They followed this game with another triumph at home in midweek, beating Leicester City 3-1 in the League Cup second round.

With all eyes on Man Utd after their stuttering start, Ipswich will see this as an ideal opportunity to ruffle the feathers of a Premier League heavyweight and further dent their sky-high ambitions.

Kick-off is at 16:30, with team news coming shortly.

#1480. What Tom Brady's exit means for Birmingham City: Why NFL legend quit St Andrew's, 'body coach' Alex Guerrero's future role revealed - and impact on Knighthead's ambitious £2bn plans for Premier League push and new stadium

Published: 08:41 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 11:15 EST, 10 November 2026

Tom Brady has quit Birmingham but his influence will continue to be felt around the Championship leaders through one of his closest allies.

The club announced via a social media post late on Monday that the NFL legend’s three-year association with Blues would end.

Titled ‘Tom Brady Departure’, the 62-word statement read: ‘Birmingham City Football Club expresses its sincere gratitude to Tom Brady for his involvement with and unwavering support for the club over the last three years.

'It was truly amazing to have someone with Tom's experience and passion associated with the club, and the club looks forward to continuing to build on that foundation from the training ground to the Birmingham community.’

Yet it can be revealed that the ideas of Brady’s ‘body coach’ Alex Guerrero will continue to inform Blues’ push for Premier League football.

Here Daily Mail Sport looks at the reasons for Brady’s departure – and what the future holds for Blues now he has gone...

Tom Brady (right) has left Birmingham City - though their plans remain ambitious under owners Knighthead and chairman Tom Wagner (left)

Brady brought stardust with him to Birmingham and was the figurehead of a new era at the club - despite attending just four matches since buying into Blues

Brady has not been a visible presence in Birmingham for about two years and attended only four matches after he was unveiled as a ‘minority investor’ in 2023, not long after US investors Knighthead had completed their takeover.

It has proved challenging for Brady to divide his time between Birmingham and his commitments in the US, where he has a £280million contract as Fox Sports main NFL analyst. He has also been part-owner of the Las Vegas Raiders since 2024.

Daily Mail Sport understands, however, that Guerrero’s methods will still be used at Blues – a significant detail given his long-term association with Brady.

Described by Brady as his 'body coach', the pair have worked together for two decades and Brady credits Guerrero with extending his NFL career beyond his 45th birthday. With Guerrero at his side, Brady won four Super Bowls and three MVP (Most Valuable Player) awards.

Birmingham chiefs have been very impressed with Guerrero, who they believe has transformed the club’s approach to fitness and recovery.

Since Guerrero came in with Brady, recovery sessions the day after a game have been mandatory and players have had individual conditioning programmes, including tailored advice on nutrition.

Daily Mail Sport understands the methods of Brady's 'body coach' Alex Guerrero (left) will still be used at Blues

In 2025, skipper Christoph Klarer told Daily Mail Sport: ‘We have so many physios and massage therapists who show you exercises in the gym and treat you before and after training. There will always be a physio available at the training ground if I want to see one. That’s not typical.’

Klarer and fellow defender Phil Neumann have not missed a game through injury as Blues players since joining in 2024 and 2025 respectively.

There have been subtle changes, though. Many of the logos and messages from TBRx – Brady’s performance and fitness company – have disappeared from the walls of the training ground in rural Warwickshire. They will be replaced by branding for the recently-launched ‘Keep Right On’ initiative as well as messages that boss Chris Davies believes are particularly relevant to his squad.

At this stage, certainly not. Knighthead remain determined to push forward their vision for Blues, with the £2billion Sports Quarter project at its heart.

The centrepiece of the Sports Quarter is the Powerhouse – a 62,000-seat stadium development that Blues hope will be one of the best in the country.

Blues may have lost their most famous face but all indications are that Brady’s departure is not a sign of Knighthead scaling back their commitment. The US group still believe Birmingham can become one of England’s most prominent clubs and are hugely excited by their progress this term, with Davies’ men top of the Championship heading into the November international break.

Knighthead still believe Birmingham can become one of England’s most prominent clubs and are hugely excited by their progress this term

Chris Davies’ men are top of the Championship heading into the November international break

It is easy to categorise Brady as a mere figurehead but that would be unfair. The 2025 Amazon Prime docuseries Built In Birmingham: Brady & The Blues was streamed in about 200 countries. There is no doubt that Brady’s presence helped Blues push certain transfer deals over the line, with Brady conducting video calls with targets. Earlier this season, Davies was late for a press conference because he had been on the phone to Brady.

The 49-year-old had a good relationship with the squad, too. He developed a strong rapport with former Blues forward Alfie May and even appeared on a FaceTime call during the wedding of May’s brother.

Equally, it would be unwise to exaggerate Brady’s role. If Blues win promotion this term, it will be a combination of Knighthead’s investment and the work of Davies and his players. By elevating the club’s profile globally, perhaps Brady has already done his job. Now it is time for the class of 2026 to write their own story.

During the early part of Brady’s time at St Andrew’s, the club leaned heavily into their rivalry with Wrexham, who are owned by Hollywood star Ryan Reynolds and his fellow actor Rob McElhenney.

When Blues took on Wrexham in September 2024, their 3-1 win was almost a sideshow. As well as the three famous Americans, David Beckham was also at St Andrew’s. When the clubs met, the US stars traded friendly insults before and after the match, generating a great deal of attention on social media.

David Beckham (right) was among the famous faces to take in a Birmingham game alongside Brady

Knighthead remain determined to push forward their vision for Blues, with the £2billion Sports Quarter project at its heart. The centrepiece is the Powerhouse – a 62,000-seat stadium

There was less of this when Blues won 2-1 at Wrexham earlier this season and perhaps that was no coincidence. There have certainly been those at Blues who feel that, at times, the club bought into the Wrexham rivalry a little too much and that forging their own path might be more fruitful.

There is no suggestion that Brady pushed the links with Wrexham yet if he is no longer associated with Blues, they may decline naturally.

In Brady’s first season, Blues were relegated to League One, with the NFL star admitting the club had tried to change too much, too soon. The appointment of Wayne Rooney was the highest-profile of those errors.

Brady departs with the club as healthy as it has been for some time. Even if he was rarely central to that recovery, he deserves at least some of the credit for it.

#1479. California votes to give record $8.4 billion to medical research

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Students, researchers and others at the University of California, Los Angeles, have protested over cuts to science funding made by the administration of US President Donald Trump during the past two years.Credit: Robyn Beck/AFP via Getty

Voters in California have approved US$8.4 billion in funding for immunology research — the largest ever infusion of cash for science authorized by a public vote in US history.

The funding proposal, known as Proposition 38, appeared on the ballot for voters in California in last week’s US mid-term elections, but it has taken nearly a week for officials to count enough ballots to declare it a success. The state government will pay for the research — which aims to find treatments that harness or re-engineer the body’s immune system to fight illnesses such as cancer and Alzheimer’s disease — by selling state government bonds. (This is unusual for science funding. Bonds are typically reserved to pay for infrastructure projects such as road construction and require the state to pay back its debt with interest.)

‘Historic change’: what the 2026 US mid-term election results mean for science

‘Historic change’: what the 2026 US mid-term election results mean for science

Supporters of the proposal say that the funding will provide stability for researchers in California, who have been affected by political turmoil. The administration of US President Donald Trump has pushed for massive cuts to science funding; put political appointees in charge of grant decisions at federal science agencies such as the US National Institutes of Health; and forced policy change at US universities that receive federal funding, including those in California.

The $8.4 billion “is an advantage to California that is unprecedented”, says Antoni Ribas, a cancer researcher and physician at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), who supported Proposition 38. It will make the state “even more of a global hub for immunology research”.

But the proposal has sparked debate. That’s because it calls for about half of the funding to be given directly to research institutes — and the only institute that matches the criteria called for in the proposal is one co-founded by Gary Michelson, a billionaire medical-device inventor. He wrote the proposition and donated about $45 million of his own funds to get it placed on the ballot and to campaign for its passage.

“I feel like the voters have been taken advantage of,” says Sarah Hill, a political scientist at California State University in Fullerton, who tracks the state’s ballot measures. Michelson did not respond to Nature’s request for comment before this story was published, but has said elsewhere that he will not personally profit from the bond revenue.

In California, citizens can place proposed laws directly on the election ballot by collecting hundreds of thousands of voter signatures.

The state has funded scientific research through this process before. In 2004, after then president George W. Bush restricted federal funding for human embryonic stem-cell research, voters in California approved a $3-billion bond to establish the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine, which they then voted to replenish with another $5.5 billion in 2020.

A campaign mailer encouraging California voters to support Proposition 38.Credit: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty

“The model works,” Ribas says. Immunologists have been making great strides with medicines such as personalized treatments called CAR-T therapies, which are revolutionizing care, he says. There has also been a flurry of research into developing vaccines, including the mRNA shots that have been the target of funding cuts by the Trump administration. Proposition 38 will ensure that such research can continue regardless of the political headwinds, Ribas adds.

Around $4 billion from Proposition 38 will fund grants for researchers at select public universities and non-profit institutes in California through a competitive review process. According to the proposal, any commercialized therapies developed through funded research must be sold at a 20% discount to people in California, with 10% of drug royalties returning to the state’s general fund.

#1478. The numbers suggest Chelsea are pushovers as they slide down the Premier League table... and club legend GUS POYET says it's time to prove they're up for a fight

Published: 07:38 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 11:44 EST, 10 November 2026

Morgan Rogers insisted it was no intentional drive-by. That he did not mean to knee Trai Hume in the head while the Sunderland defender was sitting up after a foul. Just an accident, honest.

The history shared between these two particular players opened the incident to interpretation.

Hume had folded Rogers like a deckchair in a 1-1 draw for Aston Villa last season. The challenge went viral. Sunderland shared it on their social media, glamourising it. Rogers responded at the time by saying: 'Great message to send out. Dangerous tackles getting highlight reels.'

At the Stadium of Light on Sunday, Hume was starting to sit up when Rogers caught him. Chelsea were losing 1-0, and frustrated. Their £117million arrival from Villa apologised immediately, so we will believe him when he says it was an innocent collision rather than retribution.

Nevertheless, Rogers does have an aggressive side to him. He squared up with Declan Rice at Arsenal, and James Tarkowski at Everton, and was signed in the summer partially for that passion.

Rogers has contested more duels than any other Chelsea player this season. He loses more than he wins, but is involved, for better or worse. He is Xabi Alonso's most-fouled footballer, while nobody has committed more fouls than this 6ft 2in England international.

Morgan Rogers (right) showed some fight during Chelsea's loss at Sunderland that appears to be lacking across the whole squad

If Rogers' team-mates showed the same mentality they may have avoided defeat on Sunday

Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso needs his side to develop an aggressive streak

So when we ponder whether Alonso's Chelsea are pushovers, Rogers is arguably an exception. He is a hard nut surrounded by a soft shell, and that was a problem at Sunderland.

It was not only that Brian Brobbey bullied Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana. Regis Le Bris' side were all at it, a team of bouncers ready to rough up the lads planning to party. Cole Palmer and Co ended up getting tossed out of the Stadium of Light on their rears. Chelsea recorded 69 per cent possession - their highest of the Premier League season so far - but were second-best throughout.

Gus Poyet saw that. He played for Chelsea, managed Sunderland, and was an assistant to Dennis Wise at Leeds, who will be the next visitors to Stamford Bridge after this international break.

Daniel Farke's side have won more duels and aerial duels than any other Premier League team this season, which, given what we witnessed on Sunday, should be a concern for Alonso.

Poyet can predict what is coming. Chelsea-Leeds is already a fixture with a narrative attached. It never needs a second invitation to be talked up as 'dirty'. Alonso's side will need to show a willingness to compete if that awaits, more than they managed when travelling to Sunderland.

'Sunderland went to the game with that old-fashioned mentality,' the 58-year-old Uruguayan told Daily Mail Sport. 'Pressure from the fans, noise, tackling, "I'm gonna run over you". Chelsea went on to try to play. There was quite a big difference in that aggression. We see teams that are looking so much for an identity that they forget the process to win games.'

Poyet brought up Chelsea's 2-0 win at Everton last month. We told him how Alonso had admitted it was his favourite performance of the season, describing it as 'solid' and 'serious'.

'There you go,' said Poyet, who thinks before travelling to the Stadium of Light, it would have been worth showing Chelsea's players videos from that victory at the Hill Dickinson. It was a rare showing of seriousness from Alonso's side. Only David Moyes' Everton, with 83, have committed fewer fouls than Chelsea's 95 in the Premier League this season. While giving away free-kicks is hardly a cause for celebration, it is not the worst way of measuring whether you are there to push or be pushed.

Sunderland striker Brian Brobbey (left) bulled Chelsea's Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana (right)

'For me that was a proper old-fashioned game, being able to win like that,' Poyet said about Chelsea's win at Everton. 'Put the video on and say, "Play the same".

'Now I know what the other side are going to say after watching the Sunderland game. Leeds will be saying, 'Let's go'. Leeds are very solid, and very aggressive, so it can be that kind of game.

'More and more, through the years, I think from the pandemic to now, the difference between the teams is mental. Identity, positions, shapes, blah, blah, blah, but when they are right in here (in the head), it's big. Right now, Leeds, as a team, are a little ahead mentally.'

Alonso is a polite manager. Given the chance to have a pop at the refereeing at the Stadium of Light - how Chelsea were not awarded a penalty when Cole Palmer was sandwiched, but Sunderland were when Brobbey dropped down in front of Colwill - he declined. The Blues boss chose instead to decry his team's defending as substandard. Colwill was hooked at half-time, while there were two new summer signings in the back line in Marco Palestra and Pep Chavarria who need to get to grips with the Premier League, sooner rather than later.

Poyet's first appearance after signing for Chelsea in 1997 was in the Charity Shield. Roy Keane welcomed him to English football with a kick to the head - with a little less subtlety than Rogers' knee on Hume. It finished 1-1 before Manchester United won on penalties.

Ex-Chelsea midfielder Gus Poyet has warned them of the threat Leeds pose later this month

Poyet learned a harsh lesson in that match, and not only from Keane's high kick. 'I couldn't get in the pace of the game,' Poyet recalls. 'I was always late. Ruud (Gullit) at half-time told me, "Gus, you're not really in the front, not really at the back". I said, "I'm trying!" The game was too fast.'

In a weird way, an ACL injury suffered by Poyet helped. He used the recovery time to prepare for returning. 'I went to the stadium, I was watching, learning the language, listening to Dennis Wise in the dressing room, getting that mentality,' he said. 'Then when I came back, I knew everything.

'That was my mentality. Some players need time. Some adjust quickly. You need to use all the time. For example, use this game against Sunderland when you play against Leeds. You cannot say, 'We didn't expect it'. Expect it! It's going to be similar.'

#1477. Messi was a deity among Argentina’s unholy rabble

Little sorcerer calls time on playing for his country six weeks after World Cup final defeat which was marred by brutality of his team-mates

Oliver Brown leads coverage of the greatest events in sport all over the world. He has reported on multiple Olympic Games, World Cups, Ashes series and Super Bowls, plus all major golf and tennis tournaments. His awards include Sports Feature Writer of the Year and Sports Interviewer of the Year. He was named Sports Journalist of the Year in 2024 by the London Press Club. You can find him on X at @oliverbrown_tel.

Oliver Brown leads coverage of the greatest events in sport all over the world. He has reported on multiple Olympic Games, World Cups, Ashes series and Super Bowls, plus all major golf and tennis tournaments. His awards include Sports Feature Writer of the Year and Sports Interviewer of the Year. He was named Sports Journalist of the Year in 2024 by the London Press Club. You can find him on X at @oliverbrown_tel.

Lionel Messi’s haunted expression told you more than a three-page retirement statement, artfully displayed alongside a golden pen, ever could. Sobbing and desolate under a cloudless New Jersey sky, he understood that his last game for Argentina had also been among his worst.

Where four years earlier he had adorned the greatest World Cup final with two goals, he found no artistry to salvage this abomination of an encore, drifting into anonymity while his team-mates triggered a bare-knuckle brawl. No wonder he stood apart while Leandro Paredes and Nahuel Molina did their worst, preferring to absorb one more chorus of adoration from the blue-and-white disciples before forsaking the stage for good.

You could make the case that Messi, as captain of an unholy rabble that had sought only to kick lumps out of Spain, should have taken a moral lead by hauling his team-mates into line, rather than reducing himself to their level by agitating to have Marc Cucurella sent off.

And yet for 20 years, the little sorcerer stayed aloof from his nation’s most lurid antics on the pitch, establishing himself as a strangely beatific presence on whom the highest ideals could be projected. Anybody who has heard Messi’s name being chanted by 50,000 fervent Argentines would have felt it. He was as close as 21st-century sport has come to a secular deity, the object of such veneration that Pope Francis felt compelled to remind Catholics that it was sacrilegious to keep calling him God.

Today, with one agonised announcement, that glorious delirium is over, and already Argentina seems not to know what to do with itself. Pablo Giralt, a sports anchor in Buenos Aires, was unable even to speak when he heard the news live on air, while shattered young fans described how they had called their parents in tears.

Everybody had known the moment was approaching, given the finality of his exit from the final and the subsequent death of his father, Jorge, but it still triggered an unbearable sense of loss.

Messi was the force who galvanised a nation, propelling his side from the unfathomable low of defeat to Saudi Arabia at the 2022 World Cup to holding the trophy aloft 26 days later. Who could ever hope to emulate him, to detonate such joy that the team’s homecoming bus parade in the capital had to be abandoned for a helicopter ride because of the millions on the streets?

“Thank you, God, for making me Argentine,” Messi wrote in his earnest sign-off, his strength of allegiance unfailing to the end. As a veteran of 207 international matches, with his last at La Bombonera distinguished by an ecstatic ovation, he understood both the passions he unleashed among his people and the extent to which his own story became that of an entire country.

You struggled to imagine what life was like in the eye of this madness, with his every move stalked. For the wonder of Messi was that the cult went beyond borders, that the joy he inspired across six World Cups made him beloved to billions. An abiding memory of the 2022 final is of the walk back to the metro station in Doha, where thousands of Nepalese and Bangladeshi supporters, all part of the vast migrant workforce that had built the stadiums, united in “Messi, Messi” refrains even at 1am.

Messi was majestic at that tournament, so imperious in filleting Croatia in the semi-finals that Argentina’s TV reporters abandoned even the pretence of objectivity. “Truly, you made your mark in everyone’s life, and that to me is beyond winning any World Cup,” gushed Sofia Martinez of Television Publica. And when he won it all, the mark only deepened. To occupy any press box at the World Cup where Argentina were involved this summer was to see South American colleagues in “Messi 10” jerseys, helplessly in thrall to his greatness.

As a 39-year-old, he confounded every expectation, scoring a hat-trick against Algeria and breaking Miroslav Klose’s World Cup goals record. Even when engineering those implausible fightbacks against Egypt and England, he held a volatile team together with a minimum of fuss.

Lionel Messi: #FIFAWorldCup edition 🇦🇷🌟 pic.twitter.com/E2xOh3Iose

To study Messi at his last World Cup was to see a man spared the obligation to do anything off the ball. For large periods of each game, the most minutely scrutinised athlete on the planet would do little besides wander around, only to ignite when it mattered most. You saw it in the fateful semi-final with England, where, at 1-0 down, he sloped off to the right touchline as if absent-mindedly gardening. Except he was plotting his opponents’ downfall, working out the precise spots from which to unleash two sumptuous crosses and shatter English hearts.

That alchemy would elude him in the final, where Argentina’s bid for immortality brought only instant notoriety, not to mention £236,000 in fines for misconduct. Was Messi’s image hurt by his connection to the chaos? Not in the long run. Nobody likes to cling to the fact that Pelé’s swansong for Brazil was a drawn friendly with Yugoslavia, or that Diego Maradona bowed out of World Cup football by failing a drug test for ephedrine. What endure are the indelible masterpieces those players bequeathed en route.

It will be the same for Messi, a genius defined less by his ending than by the electrifying adrenalin rush he produced along the way, spanning three finals, 21 goals, and countless flourishes to take the breath away. “Thank you” was all he had left to say. And yet the gratitude, ultimately, is all ours.

#1476. The little-known new face called up by England: Can you name the star brought in to replace Ezri Konsa?

Published: 05:58 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 12:26 EST, 10 November 2026

Thomas Tuchel has made a first-time England call-up to replace Ezri Konsa - but casual fans could be forgiven if they do not recognise the latest Three Lions addition.

He is not a widely-recognised face among the stars from the Premier League and other top European leagues in Tuchel's selection but James Hill, 24, has starred for Bournemouth in their eight-match winning run under Marco Rose this season.

The central defender, who started his career at Fleetwood Town, has enjoyed a dream few months: He married partner Tara Rose in June, welcomed his first child in August and has now had his maiden England call.

England announced today that Arsenal defender Konsa will not be in contention to face Croatia at Wembley on Thursday night - although he will be fit to potentially face Spain away on Sunday - and Hill has been called up in his place.

Hill has played for England's Under 20s and Under 21s but this is his first senior call. He was signed by Bournemouth for just £1.2million in 2022 - beating Sheffield United, Burnley, Leeds, Southampton, Tottenham and even Barcelona, who all checked on his progress.

Bournemouth's official X account posted today: 'Congratulations, Hilly. Our defender has earned a first senior @England call-up.'

James Hill - pictured with new wife Tara - has been called up to the latest England squad (Source: Instagram/james_hill_10)

Hill has starred for Bournemouth in their eight-match winning run under Marco Rose

Hill's route to the top is a fascinating one. He attended a trial day at Fleetwood as a 14-year-old and managed to impress them enough to earn place at their new academy.

Interestingly, Hill did not play for a football team of any kind before he was 10, simply kicking a ball around with friends and playing in the garden to hone his skills.

Blackpool opted against signing him after a trial and he was then dropped by Bolton after a short stint.

It proved to be a shrewd piece of talent identification from Fleetwood, with Hill later becoming the club's record sale, eclipsing the fee they received for Jamie Vardy.

And having signed for the Cherries in 2022, Hill has now established himself as a key member of Marco Rose's side.

He's played every minute of every Premier League match this season at the heart of the defence and clearly Tuchel has been impressed.

Speaking before his call-up, Hill said: 'It’s every kid’s dream, isn’t it? You grow up watching the Three Lions on TV, for the World Cup, the Euros. It’s one of the greatest honours you can have in football.'

Football is in the blood for Hill. His father, Matt, made more than 550 appearances in the Football League for the likes of Preston North End, Wolverhampton Wanderers, Sheffield United and Queens Park Rangers as a defender.

Hill played for England at age group level, pictured here kissing his now wife after a game

Hill's younger brother, Tyler, is also in the game, playing for Torquay United in National League South.

But Matt did not pressure his sons into the sport, with James previously telling the Times: 'He didn’t want me to feel as though it’s a job.

'He wanted me to feel like I’m wanting to be here because I love doing it. This is my passion. It brings me happiness. He wanted me to come to that conclusion, not for him to make that decision for me.'

Hill was a well-rounded sportsman and his secondary school did not even play football. Instead, he excelled as a fly-half for the rugby side and impressed as a javelin thrower.

He attributes his success as being aided by trying his hand at different disciplines and it is paying off in abundance having had to largely bide his time before earning a first-team spot under Andoni Iraola last term, with loans to Blackburn and Hearts helping him develop.

Hill's progress flew somewhat under the radar somewhat for many fans outside of Bournemouth and his career peak of an England call-up coincides with domestic bliss.

Having married Tara in the summer, they welcomed their daughter Edie two months later.

Hill, pictured, heading the ball away against Ipswich has become one of the best defenders in the Premier League

'Becoming a dad is one of the most special things I’ve ever experienced in my life,' he said. 'There isn’t a manual though, it’s just like, "Congratulations, you’ve got a baby". Then the door shuts! Hang on a minute. What am I supposed to do next? Is there a book for this? My wife has been absolutely incredible.'

He regularly shares pictures from both his professional and personal life on social media, putting wedding snaps alongside action shots of Bournemouth games.

Hill's England call-up will no doubt introduce him to a whole new audience previously unaware of the defender's capabilities, with only 34,000 Instagram followers at present.

The 24-year-old must now impress Tuchel enough to earn some game time when England play Croatia on Thursday in their next Nations League encounter.

#1475. Why your physics project needs an anthropologist

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Jaco de Swart is a historian and anthropologist of science at the University of Cambridge, UK.

The TAMBO team assesses suitable observatory sites in the Andes Mountains of Peru.Credit: Jaco de Swart

It is uncommon for a social scientist to have a seat at a meeting about an astronomical observatory, let alone for them to jointly lead one. For one-quarter of attendees to be social-science scholars is almost unprecedented. But that’s exactly what happens at meetings about the Tau Air-shower Mountain-based Observatory (TAMBO), a proposed detector to be built in the Peruvian Andes to look for cosmic particles called tau neutrinos.

Space diplomacy: bridging the operating gaps between myriad missions

Space diplomacy: bridging the operating gaps between myriad missions

Tau neutrinos are elusive fundamental particles that are transmitted through space from black holes and other distant sources. When these particles interact with rocks on Earth, they can produce a shower of other, short-lived particles. The idea behind TAMBO is that if such a shower were emitted from one side of a deep canyon, it could be picked up by an array of 5,000 detectors on the other side (TAMBO collaboration. Nature Astron. 10, 947–951; 2026). The Andes Mountains of Peru contain many promising sites.

For those who live in the area, however, the case for TAMBO is less clear. The Andes are a sensitive ecological environment and home to Indigenous farming communities that consider the mountains sentient beings that are integral to their society. The area is also affected by legal and illegal mining, large-scale infrastructure projects and legacies of colonialism. This all leads to scepticism towards large projects that are developed by people from outside the area.

I am the co-principal investigator of the TAMBO collaboration, alongside Peruvian neutrino physicist Carlos Argüelles at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts. I lead the social-science and ‘responsible siting’ side of the project. Having received funding to build a proof-of-principle experiment called TAMBITO, we are searching for a potential location for the observatory.

Developing astronomers in Africa: ‘We wanted to create a discipline’

Developing astronomers in Africa: ‘We wanted to create a discipline’

Since 2024, the TAMBO collaboration has built partnerships with 11 Peruvian institutions, which are involved in the design and development of the telescope. Scientific links are an important starting point, but they are not enough. No matter what their discovery potential is, big scientific experiments are not beneficial to everyone. For example, construction of the Thirty Meter Telescope has been stalled since 2015 because of protests triggered by objections to its planned site on Maunakea in Hawaii — a mountain that is sacred in Native Hawaiian culture.

To integrate environmental care into the project and build good relationships with the communities that might host the telescope, TAMBO brought in experts on the Andean region. In 2024, the collaboration held a workshop at Harvard’s Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study, at which scholars and policymakers discussed what equitable astrophysics in Peru would look like. This led to the formation of a responsible-siting team that includes geographers, sociologists and anthropologists who have worked in the Andes.

IceCube just won a Nobel prize. Protect astroparticle physics projects with the same potential
