#1420. Outstanding Leeds cut short Jaissle’s Newcastle honeymoon

The noise started in a corner of the South Stand, early in the second half. It was muffled at first, but as the ball popped from one white shirt to another, it became louder and louder, sweeping around the stadium: here was the soundtrack for a humiliation.

“Olé! Olé! Olé!” they roared and why not? Leeds were ripping Newcastle to pieces, knocking passes around them as if they were training-ground mannequins. Football has become a sport that leaves people increasingly vexed, but this was a night when – for the locals, at least – it was almost a throwback.

There was energy and ferocious tackling, a No 9 soaring like centre-forwards used to in the not-too-distant past and lots of goals as Leeds cut loose and abruptly ended whatever honeymoon Matthias Jaissle had been experiencing in charge of Newcastle.

“I suppose in football you can always find something to moan about,” Daniel Farke, the Leeds manager, said. “But this was a top-class performance.”

It has felt suspiciously like Newcastle’s start has been like an overstuffed plastic shopping bag, the handles straining to the point of snapping. Eventually they fell asunder. Leeds ran all over them and were too smart, slick and hungry, not to mention ruthless. No wonder Jaissle had nowhere to go.

The home fans were adamant this was one of the best nights Leeds have experienced under Farke and if they were prepared to say as much, you had an obligation to listen. Forget how wretched Newcastle were, Leeds had produced a performance to enable imaginations to run wild.

Centre to it all was Ao Tanaka, with his desire to keep Leeds playing forward, but it felt wrong to talk about one man when you had the unstoppable Dominic Calvert-Lewin, who would be substituted to a standing ovation, and the ubiquitous James Justin, among others.

"He just cannot stop scoring at Elland Road" 🔥Dominic Calvert-Lewin makes it 2-0 to Leeds! pic.twitter.com/Pv1TEpc5Qj

The foundations are being put in around the stadium for a cavernous new West Stand, and Farke’s remit is to ensure that Leeds will be firmly established in the Premier League by the time it is completed in the summer of 2028.

To be fair to Farke, he has laid a sturdy base for this team to thrive and it felt before kick-off that this was going to be a big evening for Leeds, who had made a quietly encouraging start to the campaign and had negotiated three challenging away trips without defeat.

Big? It turned out to be spectacular. The first half was so one-sided that a boxing referee would not have allowed Newcastle to come out for the second, such was the pummelling they received; wave after wave of white-shirted raids left the visitors black and blue.

Aside from one little rick inside the opening 10 minutes, when James Trafford dithered and presented Yoane Wissa with a chance to mug him, Leeds were every bit as sensational as Newcastle were shocking, seizing on the opportunity to go on a rampage.

Leeds would have been in front after 11 minutes but Ethan Ampadu’s fierce drive battered into Calvert-Lewin’s legs and bounced away. Normally in such circumstances, players will wave an arm to berate their bad luck, but Ampadu, celebrating his 26th birthday, smiled: he, like everyone else, sensed what was coming.

Jayden Bogle, Justin and Nico Elvedi all had opportunities to open the scoring earlier, but eventually, they found the weak spot. Newcastle, who had lost the influential Nico González to a potential concussion, had replaced him with Sean Steur and what an influence he would have on matters.

On the half hour, Steur was a fraction too late getting out to close down Tanaka, whose shot ricocheted off him and to Lewis Miley, before looping away from Lukas Hornicek and dropping into the corner of the net in dam-busting fashion.

Ao Tanaka's deflected effort puts Leeds ahead! ⚪ pic.twitter.com/cYXVi3LOAO

Leeds were running even quicker by this point, pressing as if their lives depended on it and making tackles that were lustily acclaimed in the stands. Steur completely short-circuited in the bedlam and a ridiculous pass on the edge of his area was pounced upon by Bogle.

Out went a ball to Justin, whose cross was whipped into the penalty area, where Calvert-Lewin had climbed to get his head to it, though replays indicated his effort glanced off Bogle’s head – determining the true scorer will make for an interesting conversation.

Calvert-Lewin, at least, got the reward his efforts deserved on the cusp of half-time, spinning away from Miley and chopping inside Sven Botman before delivering the kind of finish that should make Thomas Tuchel take note when selecting his next England squad this week.

"They are relentless!"Dominic Calvert-Lewin caps off a dominant first-half from Leeds 💪 pic.twitter.com/S6kQykOMW9

The gloss, after those “olés”, was applied in the 59th minute when Noah Okafor put a realistic hue on the score, ramming in a finish in front of the Kop and leaving Newcastle open to the crudest mocking for the amount of money they have spent to resemble such a disorganised rabble.

A wonderful strike with equally brilliant celebrations from Noah Okafor! 🕺 pic.twitter.com/Ce1ueKtH4x

Bazoumana Touré, at least, scored a consolation goal, but Jaissle barely flickered as it went in and the emotion belonged to Farke, who thundered on to the pitch at the final whistle and sought out his captain, Ampadu, who had erred in allowing Newcastle’s substitute to profit.

“That was an unnecessary goal to concede and I so wanted us to keep a clean sheet,” Farke sighed. “We deserved a clean sheet and I couldn’t help myself. I had to tell him because I am sometimes a perfectionist. We must try to stay humble, but we can be an outstanding team.”

And this, for certain, was an outstanding night.

[It was brutal out there?] That’s football. That’s the Premier League. It was clear from the start and I have said it many times. We will have ups and downs and challenges all the way. Tonight we faced that challenge. It’s tough and difficult to digest. But there is a chance to learn out of that and there’s a long time until our next match at home and that is good.

It’s clear with our young squad that there will be ups and downs and you have to bring the fundamentals on the pitch against such a physical team. Leeds are so intense, we couldn’t match that physicality. There are other aspects of course but I don’t want to make excuses. We want to learn out of it and be better.

[Were you overwhelmed as a team?] No. If you don’t bring that physicality on the pitch, you struggle.

Exactly this [message to the players]. Bring your fundamentals and we build on it. [Can you bounce back from this in your next game?] Of course. [Is your confidence hit?] No

For each manager it would be a nightmare after such a game to concede so late and not have the well-deserved clean sheet. Of course I was not happy about the situation. Doesn’t take anything away from my boys who were magnificent. Terrific start with eight points but there’s never a perfect performance. There’s always something to moan about. At very rare points [in the season] I have to criticise [for conceding].

Energy, quality, good structure, in an out of possession, which is complicated against Newcastle, In pressing them you always have to be aware of their unbelievable pace and strength in counter-attacks. We found this balance today and in the first half particularly we were dominant.

We have a good fitness level now. Need to find the right triggers to press. It’s a lot of well-structured work on the training ground. We had more chances to score tonight but overall I am very happy with our performance.

[Calvert-Lewin being praised] It is well deserved. He is in outstanding shape and plays with lots of confidence. I expect him to lead the group with some other players. His work-rate is never in doubt and to me he is one of the best strikers in the league.

The ref told me at half-time that they’ve taken it off me. I didn’t know he [Bogle] was there to be fair. I just got up and went ‘Bang!’ It is what it is. I’ll take the assist!

I didn’t know anything about it [being given credit for the second goal]. I said to the ref, I don’t fancy telling him [Calvert-Lewin]. To be fair he’s still raging. He’s raging with the goal but happy with the result.

It’s about having an understanding with the players around you. With Dom up there, you know he’s going to win everything so you have to get the runners around him.

It’s about the rotation like today. When James Justin goes wider there’s space inside. Dom occupies two centre-backs so there’s always pockets.

Regardless of the scoreline it was a tough game physically. They’re a very good side. We take it game by game, not to get carried away. Everyone’s ambitious in their own way but we have to take it game by game.

A proper stuffing for Newcastle as Leeds continue to impress and climb up to third.

James pounces on a loose ball, dribbles infield from the right. No one bothers to close him down so he eventually has a shot, blazing over with his left from 20 yards.

Late free-kick for Leeds after Livramento bundled Aaronson over. Wilson chips from the left to the far post and Muharemovic heads it back acros goal looking for a team-mate but none had made the run.

Leeds 4 Newcastle 1 (Touré) No clean sheet for Leeds. Farke is fuming after the substitute exploits an error and scores with a left-foot shot that deflects off Justin.

Livramento drives the ball 60 yards looking for Barnes but the ball skids off the turf and into Trafford’s arms.

Crunching Bard tackle on Bamba sends the ball to James who lets fly from 22 yards into the shins of a Newcastle defender.

Bard is penalised for a trip on Barnes as the game peters out.

Ampadu and Bamba collide when fighting for a loose ball but there was nothing malicious in it.

Wissa escapes a booking for a snide kick at Muharemovic’s shin.

A debatable offside call which should have been left for VAR lets Trafford off the hook when he comes out of his area to clear a ball clipped over the top. He slices it to Toure and the ref stops the game but I think Bard was playing Wissa, who found Toure, onside.

Newcastle corner on the left headed out by Elvedi and Barnes recovers the ball to start another attack with the 18-yard line stacked with players. When the diagonal comes back from left to right Barnes heads it behind for a goalkick.

Willock hooks a half-volley on to the roof of the net.

Bard → GudmundssonAaronson → OkaforWilson → Tanaka

Newcastle free-kick for a trip on Willock. Hall takes and Leeds head it out for a throw-in.

Livramento improves the quality of crosses with two that at least find the middle of the box even if they were headed away by Elvedi and Justin respectively.

Newcastle are enjoying more possession but the crossing has been awful when they do get down the flanks, Touré the latest offender.

Barnes shoots down Trafford’s throat. Barnes had thrown himself down in the box moments earlier and there was a VAR check but there was nothing like the contact required to send him swan-diving on to the grass.

Wissa gets down the right and whips over a low cross but Willock’s touch was too heavy.

There was a piece in the Athletic today saying Newcastle pivoted to Hornicek instead of pursuing Trafford again because he had a very high ceiling and was younger. He hasn’t caught much here, dropping the ball even when he chooses not to punch.

Matthias Jaissle promised high intensity, high octane, front foot football when he was interviewed for the Newcastle job. He and sporting director Ross Wilson have repeated that promise several times since he was appointed. There has been no sign of it since the opening weekend against Liverpool.

Newcastle are passive, they look disorganised in midfield and weak at the back. Oh and they barely apply pressure let alone attack dangerously.

These are early days but this performance and result had been coming. A pretty brutal reality check after all the positive noise and bold predictions in pre-season. This defeat will drop Newcastle to 12th in the table, where they finished last season under Eddie Howe.

Leeds 4 Newcastle 0 (Okafor) Ampadu hurls it into the box. A defender heads it to the edge of the area where Okafor thumps a left-footed half-volley in off the right post.

A wonderful strike with equally brilliant celebrations from Noah Okafor! 🕺 pic.twitter.com/Ce1ueKtH4x

Livramento slides in to stop Okafor’s drive down the left, giving Leeds another opportunity to throw it long.

Triple change: Livramento → DedicTouré → Fernandez-PardoWillock → Murphy

Leeds catch Newcastle playing short from the back. Stach blindsides Steur 20 yards out, tackles him, cuts inside then bends a left foot shot into the side-netting.

After Hall stings Trafford’s palms with a strike from distance. Newcastle want a penalty when the ball hits Tanaka’s arm … but it was outside the area and then Murphy, in frustration, chops down Gudmundsson and takes the booking as an occupational hazard.

Elvedi sloppily gives the ball way to Wissa who tries to set Fernandez-Pardo through down the left. Justin sticks with him and Bogle mops up after Justin was tripped.

Gudmundsson does the upended beetle when he tries to break from the corner and collides with a Newcastle player. He claims he was fouled and wthrashes about like a RL player after he’s tackled. He continues to do a Rumpelstiltskin polka of peevishness towards the ref for a while.

Newcastle corner on the left that Trafford backpedals to tip behind for another.

No changes at half-time for Newcastle as they kick off. Leeds break through the middle quickly and Calvert-Lewin seems to push the ball past Botman and shapes to shoot before Steur slides in with a crucial tackle just inside the box.

The first goal is now an own goal. The explanation is that Tanaka’s shot was on target but the deflection from Steur meant it was going wide until it hit Miley.

Now the second goal has been credited to Bogle as Calvert-Lewin’s header struck the top of his head before it went in.

You could not say that this scoreline is undeserved. Newcastle are being demolished physically. The central midfield two – Steur and Miley – just don’t have the power to screen their defence.

Leeds 3 Newcastle 0 (Calvert-Lewin) Leeds are running all over Newcastle who seem physically flimsy. Calvert-Lewin chops in from the left on to a flick-on, the ball takes a deflection off the Newcastle captain and he steers it into the far corner with a right-foot shot.

"They are relentless!"Dominic Calvert-Lewin caps off a dominant first-half from Leeds 💪 pic.twitter.com/S6kQykOMW9

Calvert-Lewin is booked for catching Botman in the face with a straight arm rather than a swinging arm. ‘Reckless but not violent.’ Trafford had punchd the corner away at the back post to set Leeds off on a counter.

Tanaka gives the ball away carelessly in midfield and Newcastle work it to Wissa who chops inside past Elvedi, hangs out his own leg looking for contact and hits the deck. The ref waves play on and the ball runs to Barnes in the left of the area. He shapes to shoot but Muharemovic sprinted over to make a fine block-tackle, forcing it behind for a corner.

Newcastle are rocking here. They cannot win a tackle.

For those of us who have watched all Newcastle United’s games this season, this was coming. They do not have any consistent attacking threat, they do no create chances and they are not secure at the back either.

They’ve survived by converting the very few chances they create in games but they have not even had a shot in the first half here.

Leeds should be three up after Hornicek fumbled Gudmundsson’s shot from the left. The ball falls to Calvert-Lewin five yards out and he triesto dink it over the keeper who recovers well to smother it.

Leeds 2 Newcastle 0 (Calvert-Lewin) Newcastle try to play the ball out from the back, give it away cheaply to Bogle who feeds Justin haring down the right. He is ostensibly the right centre-back but he is a full-back by trade and stands up a perfect near-post cross that Calvert-Lewin hangs in the air to bury with the firmest of headers. In fact it transpires that his downward header struck Bogle and another deflection benefits rampant Leeds –162 seconds between the goals.

"He just cannot stop scoring at Elland Road" 🔥Dominic Calvert-Lewin makes it 2-0 to Leeds! pic.twitter.com/Pv1TEpc5Qj

Leeds 1 Newcastle 0 (Tanaka) Good move, spawny finish. Tanaka sprays a pass out to Okafor who drives at Dedic then picks out Tanaka who had held his run. He cushions the pass then lets fly. The ball hits Steur, deflects on to Miley and then loops into the right of the goal with Hornicek understandably stranded.

Ao Tanaka's deflected effort puts Leeds ahead! ⚪ pic.twitter.com/cYXVi3LOAO

Good tackle by Steur on Bogle stops the Leeds right-back flying forward after Calvert-Lewin’s flick-on.

Newcastle really are not afraid to launch the ball forward are they? Football tactics are constantly evolving and fashions come back around. What better way to play through a press than to bypass the midfield completely? The hope is it will also cause the centre-backs problems, get them facing their own goal under pressure from one of Newcastle’s rapid forward players in a foot race.

It almost worked a couple of times in the first half but it should be pointed out that the best direct/long ball teams of the past tended to have a striker who was dominant in the air. Newcastle do not currently have one which does limit their threat from flick ons.

Newcastle break from defending a long throw. Wissa carries it 60 yards but with Murphy and Fernadez-Pardo better placed, he tries to shoot from 25 yards and plinks it straight at Trafford, provoking an inevitable ‘Woooooooo’.

From the resulting long throw Elvedi is found at the back post, unmarked and attempts to volley it towards goal, missing the ball entirely. It was so wild that even the Leeds staff laugh at how inept it was.

Leeds have a corner when they use one of their signature moves, Bogle cutting in from the right across the back four to take a ball over the top. He controls it but cannot force it past Thiaw.

Hornicek claws out the corner to Bogle 18 yards out. He puts his laces through a volley that Hornicek parries up high and punches away when he has a second go.

Newcastle chip it long again, this time down the right. Gudmundsson holds off Murphy and Leeds will have the relief of a goal-kick.

Leeds are finding it hard now to play through Newcastle’s high press and the intensity with which they are hounding keeper and defenders.

Newcastle keep looking to use their pace with balls over the top for Wissa, Murphy and Fernandez-Pardo. Wissa closes Trafford down quickly again. He needs to release it with more urgency.

Gonzalez hs not recovered from being struck on the head by the ball and is being replaced by Steur as a concussion sub.

Justin heads over his own bar when Newcastle chip a long pass down the inside right. Wissa beats Muharemovic and tries to find Fernandez-Pardo but Justin got there first. Newcastle go short from the corner and Leeds force them back into their own half.

Terrific save from Hornicek down low to his right. Tanaka’s cross from the left found Justin creeping round the back on the right and heading across goal from the back post. Bogle swivelled and tried a sidewinder flick that was arrowing towards the bottom left corner until the keeper swooped to turn it away with his right hand.

Wissa is ticking, feeling he is getting nothing from the referee when challenging for the ball, the latest incident involving a collision with Justin which was 50-50.

Leeds have been the slicker of the two sides, their passing and movement causing the full-backs problems. Okafor dribbles down the left and centres. Stach lays it back to Ampadu who hammers a half-volley from 18 yards that poleaxes Calvert-Lewin who was in an offside position.

Newcastle fans sing ‘There’s only one Kevin Keegan’ as the visitors’ defence sweeps the ball around. When they knock the ball up the inisde-right channel Wissa is penalised for swinging his arm and catching Muharemovic in the mooey.

Wissa presses Trafford high and the goalkeeper is a bit too casual but gets away with it. His clearance bounces off the attacker’s shin and loops out to the right. Leeds shift it quickly out to the left with Gudmundsson and Okafor bombing forward. A vicious cross from the left-back hits a Newcastle leg, loops up and smaxks Gonzales flush in the face, knocking him off his feet. The ref stops play.

Two bad moments for Newcastle early on. Lewis Hall caught out by a simple run and pass behind him and then, from the resulting corner Mathias Fernandez-Pardo looked very fortunate, in my opinion, to avoid conceding a penalty for handball.

He got the benefit of the doubt presumably because the ball bounced up onto his hand as he tried to bring it under control and he did not intend to control it with his hand or knock it away. The handball law confuses me but there is a higher threshold now.

Stach tackles Wissa in the centre-circle. Wissa is playing behind Fernandez-Pardo. Ampadu receives a long pass over the top, coming back from an offside position in the nick of time.

Fernandez-Pardo’s outstretched left arm is struck in the penalty area with the ball after they win the header but the ref waves play on and stops the game for a foul on the new striker.

It’s never a problem to come to Elland Road and the singing of Marching On Together before kick-off makes this one of the top three atmospheres in the country, easily. There are problems with VAR, though, and the whole stadium has just seen the ball strike Matias Fernanzes-Pardo’s hand in the area. The reason it is a problem is because we have become conditioned to thinking every time a ball touches someone on the arm in the area, a penalty should be awarded. It is preposterous that faceless beaks have distorted the game so much.

Leeds kick off, attacking the South Stand, from left to right, as they always prefer to do. Justin and Bogle combine on the right and Bogle bends a pass inside HAll to Stach who chooses to cross rather than shoot. It hits Botman and goes out for a corner.

Leeds are in their home kit of white with yellow and blue pinstripe hoops, Newcastle in their navy away kit.

Anthony [Elanga] is injured. Unfortunately we have to investigate further how long he will be out but obviously we miss him. We wish him to come back as quickly as possible. It could be [a long-term injury] but he will get another MRI next week and then we’ll see.

Lewis Hall is the perfect player profile for how we play. he is a young lad still and we are very excited [that he has signed a new contract].

The start was not easy. We didn’t have lots of time to prepare for pre-season and that’s one reason we are happy and satisfied with the start. But there is potential and we will work hard on the margins we want to improve.

There will be a lot of excitement surrounding Mathias Fernandez-Pardo’s first start for Newcastle United following his deadline day move from Lille but also keep an eye on Jacob Murphy on the right wing.

Fernandez-Pardo starts with a clean slate at Newcastle, Murphy has a lot of baggage and he has been a popular online target for criticism over the last year or so.

Indeed, some sections of the fanbase were stunned Newcastle rejected a £15m offer from Nottingham Forest on deadline day for a player who has entered the final 12 months of his contract.

Murphy has his limitations, sure and he can be infuriating sometimes when he gives the ball away cheaply, but there is a reason Matthias Jaissle was adamant he could not be sold.

Part of that is due to the fact he does not have another specialist right winger behind Anthony Elanga who misses the Leeds game through injury.

But Murphy is also valued for his experience and his training ground presence. He has been at the club a long time, working under Rafa Benítez, Steve Bruce and Eddie Howe and is a boyhood Newcastle fan.

Jaissle was not willing to lose that from his dressing room. Ultimately, though, Murphy has to perform on the pitch to justify the faith shown in him.

There are not many other options to fill that position while Elanga is missing. Harvey Barnes does not like playing on the right, Amar Dedic is a full back and so is Tino Livramento.

This is an opportunity for Murphy to silence his detractors and prove the faith Jaissle has put in him is not misplaced. At the age of 31, he knows he is not the most popular or appreciated player at the club but he has never shirked or complained about that.

He formed a potent partnership with Alexander Isak when he was leading the line for Newcastle. Can he do the same with the new boy Fernandez-Pardo?

Mind you I remember his visit to Elland Road in 1982-83. Not for the faint hearted. In fact it was a disgrace when he was hit by a coin. And yet he was always gracious about Leeds and particularly fond of Don Revie. He was one of very few football people without a strong Leeds United connection who went to his funeral in 1989.

Apparently he was injured in training, the nature of the injury is unspecified.

Newcastle have made a very good start particularly in their transitional moments on the counter-attack. We have to be switched on today to get the next points.

After many years of suffering our supporters deserve it [high expectations]. It’s good but we are far away from not being humble. Our feet are on the ground. We know the second year is always difficult. We have made a good start and it is always important to ride the momentum as long as possible.

Eddie Howe has left a legacy and the culture he created is still around. Matthias has to work with it. They are unbeaten. they are very dangerous with many pacy players up front. It’s important not to lose the ball too easily and always be switched on against Newcastle.

Leeds United Trafford; Justin, Elvedi, Muharemovic; Bogle, Ampadu, Tanaka, Gudmundsson; Stach, Okafor; Calvert-Lewin. Substitutes Zetterer, Bard, Bijol, Longstaff, Aaronson, Wilson, James, Bahoya, Nmecha.

Newcastle United (4-2-3-1) Hornicek; Dedic, Thiaw, Botman, Hall; González, L Miley; Murphy, Fernandez-Pardo, Barnes; Wissa. Substitutes Pope, Livramento, Schär, Bamba, Steur, Touré, Willock, Ramsey, M Miley.

Fernández-Pardo replaces Joe Willock and Murohy comes in for Elanga from the starters of the 2-2 draw with Bournemouth:

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of Leeds United vs Newcastle United, the last Premier League match of the fourth round of fixtures for the 2026-27 season. Both clubs have made unbeaten starts with one win and two draws each and a win today for wither would send them up to fourth. The two sides met at Elland Road in the third match of last season which ended in a 0-0 draw but the return fixture at St James’ Park was one of the games of the season, a ding-dong match that Leeds led 0-1, 1-2 and 2-3, the latter until the 91st minute and yet still lost 4-3.

The architect of that victory for Newcastle was the Leeds’ fans’ incubus, a player commonly known around Elland Road as ‘Harvey F------- Barnes’. His two goals that night were his sixth and seventh against Leeds in eight matches for Leicester and the Toon. Back in the last century and at the turn of this one, Alan Shearer scored 21 league goals in 23 games against Leeds for Blackburn Rovers and Newcastle, it can feel like one bogeyman passing the baton to another.

Newcastle’s sound form with their new model team this season has been based on searing pace and their ability on the counter whether with runners, in the case of Anthony Elanga, or with long diagonals against Tottenham that ripped a hole in the left side of their defence. Leeds rallied from being overrun by Brentford at half-time in their last home game to switch from three at the back to four and wrest back the initiative and while they reverted for the Brighton draw, in both games it was the introduction of Ao Tanaka in midfield that gave them control.

It is genuinely hard to decide whether the 6-3 defeat by Chelsea in the Carabao Cup from being 2-0 up at Stamford Bridge is significant to Leeds league form. One simplistic way of looking at it would be to say Leeds reserves were better than Chelsea’s reserves in the first half and Chelsea’s first-team were better than Leeds reserves and their shaky, debutant keeper in the second. But any similar defensive frailties tonight and there will be jitters over the next week before the international break. Newcastle, by contrast, toiled in their 1-0 victory over Millwall but the result glosses over a lack of incision for long spells of it.

Joe Rodon is out for Leeds for at least another month while Newcastle have changed to withholding information about their treatment room under Matthias Jaissle who says that it should be ‘confidential’. We do know that Joelinton, William Osula and Dan Burn are likely to still be out given the nature of their injuries but Amar Dedic, who came off at half-time at the New Den with a thigh or hamstring problem, may be back.

#1419. Ice-Breakers & Idea Planning For New Junior Fans' Forum Intake

Everton’s 2026/27 Junior Fans’ Forum gathered for the first time during October half-term, with the group brainstorming initial plans and ideas for the campaign.

The youngsters, aged 11-16, met at the Blues’ Royal Liver Building headquarters for ice-breakers and to learn more about what they can expect from their meetings with the Club throughout the season.

For the first time since its inception, the Junior Fans’ Forum includes returning members this season, meaning those who were part of the initiative in 2025/26 were able to share their experiences and answer questions from the new intake.

Junior Fans’ Forum membership will continue to be staggered over two seasons going forward to allow for greater continuity year-to-year, while still creating an annual opportunity for young Evertonians to apply for the group.

The move will also enable the Club’s Fan Engagement team to collaborate with the Junior Fans’ Forum on longer-term projects and ideas aimed at younger supporters.

Last season, the group focused on raising awareness of Everton in the Community among their peers, culminating in the group working with Everton's Culinary Experiences Partner Aramark to create a one-off fundraising doughnut that was sold at the annual EitC fixture against Chelsea in March.

In recognition of their efforts, Forum members were joined by Everton defender Jake O’Brien, midfielder Charly Alcaraz and then-Blues winger Dwight McNeil for a special launch event and taste test at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

This year’s Forum members will continue to meet in school holidays throughout the season. For updates from their meetings, keep an eye on evertonfc.com/Fans!

#1418. The molecular basis of replication fork restart via repriming by PRIMPOL

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Eukaryotic genomes are exposed to numerous sources of DNA damage that impede replication. Only a decade ago, repriming by the primase–polymerase PRIMPOL was identified as a pathway that enables cells to tolerate DNA damage1,2,3,4. However, the molecular mechanism that underlies repriming remains poorly understood, and it is unclear how PRIMPOL is precisely targeted to stalled forks, where along single-stranded DNA PRIMPOL binds and how PRIMPOL is regulated to minimize error-prone DNA synthesis. Here, to dissect the molecular basis of repriming, we perform real-time single-molecule imaging in nuclear extracts that recapitulate genome maintenance. We directly visualize how stalled forks restart through repriming. We show that PRIMPOL is recruited to stalled forks through an interaction with the replicative helicase CDC45–MCM2–7–GINS (CMG). This facilitates primer handover from PRIMPOL to the high-fidelity polymerase ε, minimizing mutagenic DNA synthesis. At near-physiological concentrations, PRIMPOL reprimes leading strands in a CMG-dependent manner and polymerase ε extends those primers. This primary mode of repriming does not require DNA damage checkpoint signalling. PRIMPOL overexpression and checkpoint activation promote a secondary mode of repriming, whereby PRIMPOL restarts DNA synthesis far from CMG and polymerase δ extends those primers. Our data reveal a simple yet effective mechanism that directs PRIMPOL’s activity to stalled forks awaiting restart, and suggest a strategy to inhibit the repriming pathway.

Multiple pathways maintain genome stability during replication stress (RS)5, including fork reversal and translesion DNA synthesis (TLS)6. In 2013, a new RS response pathway called repriming was identified in eukaryotes1,2,3,4. PRIMPOL performs repriming and enables cells to tolerate diverse DNA lesions1,2,3,4,7,8. As it lacks proofreading, PRIMPOL has an error rate comparable to that of TLS polymerases (10−2−10−4)9,10. PRIMPOL-deficient cells and mice are hypersensitive to several DNA-damaging agents8,11,12,13, underscoring its role in genome maintenance. While repriming enables cancer cells to tolerate RS induced by oncogenes14 and chemotherapy15, PRIMPOL generates single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) gaps16,17 that sensitize cells to PARP inhibitors18,19,20. Blocking fork reversal enhances repriming, suggesting that cells favour high-fidelity pathways to minimize mutagenic DNA synthesis7,21,22.

The replicative helicase CMG unwinds parental DNA23 and is functionally coupled to polymerase ε (Pol ε)24, which synthesizes the leading strand. The lagging strand is primed and extended by primase–polymerase α (Pol α) and polymerase δ (Pol δ), respectively24. Damage on the lagging strand is readily bypassed due to the discontinuous nature of Okazaki fragment synthesis25,26. This is not the case for leading strand DNA lesions, which stall Pol ε while CMG continues to unwind DNA25,26,27. This CMG uncoupling exposes ssDNA that is rapidly coated by replication protein A (RPA)28. The notion that PRIMPOL may reprime leading strand synthesis was hypothesized at the time of its discovery2, and discussed in later work7,16,29, but there is no direct evidence for this idea.

Although repriming is a major RS response pathway and PRIMPOL is an attractive therapeutic target, key mechanistic aspects of repriming remain unclear. For example, although RPA recruits PRIMPOL to ssDNA30,31, it is unclear why PRIMPOL acts at stalled forks, but not on ssDNA generated by other processes (transcription, recombination). One study reported that high RPA concentrations inhibit PRIMPOL’s activity on ssDNA in vitro30, presumably because RPA fully coats ssDNA and prevents PRIMPOL’s access to the template. Another study found that RPA stimulated PRIMPOL’s activity on ssDNA long enough to accommodate the simultaneous binding of both proteins, that Pol ε can extend PRIMPOL’s primers in vitro and that RPA stimulates PRIMPOL’s enzymatic activity in synergy with Pol ε31. It remains unclear how repriming occurs in the nucleus, where RPA is abundant and rapidly coats exposed ssDNA. Although PRIMPOL is a known target of checkpoint kinase 1 (CHK1)22, how the DNA damage checkpoint regulates repriming remains poorly understood. Finally, it is unclear how PRIMPOL is regulated to minimize mutagenic DNA synthesis during repriming.

To address these questions, we used single-molecule imaging to directly visualize PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart in Xenopus egg extracts. We found that PRIMPOL preferentially binds near stalled forks, suggesting that it interacts with fork-associated proteins. We identified an interaction between PRIMPOL and CMG that is required for targeting PRIMPOL to stalled forks and for efficient fork restart in nuclear extract and in human cells. Our data indicate that the PRIMPOL–CMG interaction facilitates primer handover from PRIMPOL to the leading strand polymerase Pol ε, therefore minimizing mutagenic DNA synthesis. Finally, in conditions that mimic PRIMPOL overexpression, we found that PRIMPOL can reprime DNA synthesis far from the replicative helicase, and those primers are extended by Pol δ. Our findings support a simple-yet-elegant mechanism that targets PRIMPOL’s activity specifically to stalled forks and suggest a strategy to inhibit repriming.

To investigate the mechanism of PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart, we used nuclear extract prepared from Xenopus laevis eggs32. This extract contains all soluble nuclear proteins, supports efficient DNA replication and recapitulates several RS response pathways33. We could not detect frog PRIMPOL in egg extract using mass spectrometry (MS) or western blotting (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Table 1). To reconstitute repriming, we supplemented nuclear extract with recombinant human PRIMPOL, which displayed robust enzymatic activity in vitro (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d).

To visualize PRIMPOL-mediated fork restart in real-time, we adapted a single-molecule assay called kinetics of eukaryotic replication via molecular imaging and tracking (KERMIT)25,34. A biotinylated linear DNA template was double-tethered onto a streptavidin-coated coverslip in a microfluidic flow-cell (Fig. 1a). DNA was incubated with high-speed supernatant—an extract that supports origin licensing but not origin firing, mimicking G1 (ref. 32) (Fig. 1a). The flow-cell was washed with buffer to remove any soluble proteins while retaining DNA-bound MCM2–7. Licensed DNA was incubated with nucleoplasmic extract—an extract that supports origin firing, elongation and RS response, mimicking S phase32 (Fig. 1a). Replication was monitored in real-time using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy.

a, The single-molecule imaging workflow. b, Kymograms showing CMG dynamics at unperturbed forks. GINS–LD655 (orange) tracks the CMG helicase, and FEN1–KikG (blue) serves as a nascent DNA marker. c, CMG dynamics in aphidicolin-treated extract. d, CMG dynamics in Pol-α-depleted extract. e, CMG dynamics in Pol-α-depleted extract with 30 nM of WT PRIMPOL. The white arrows denote PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart events. f, Fork restart efficiency: the fraction of uncoupled CMGs that resumed fast translocation. Data are mean ± 95% confidence interval (CI) estimated by bootstrapping. n values denote the number of forks. g, CMG dynamics at DNA lesions in undepleted extract. The yellow arrows indicate fork stalling at the lesion. h, CMG speeds measured in different experiments. The blue lines indicate medians, shaded areas represent 95% CI estimated by bootstrapping. n values denote the number of CMG molecules. Ctrl, control. i, CMG dynamics at DNA lesions in extract + 30 nM of WT PRIMPOL. The white arrows indicate PRIMPOL-mediated restart events. The experiments shown in b–h were repeated twice with different extract preparations. j, Autoradiogram of plasmid replication assay in mock-depleted (i) versus Pol-α-depleted extract + buffer (ii), +3 nM WT PRIMPOL (iii), +10 nM WT PRIMPOL (iv), +30 nM WT PRIMPOL (v), +30 nM PRIMPOL(AxA) (vi) or +30 nM PRIMPOL(ΔRPA) (vii). The cartoons illustrate replication intermediates corresponding to bands on the gel (blue indicates nascent DNA). k, Quantification of the plasmid replication assay shown in j from three independent repeats. Total DNA synthesis (dark grey) or supercoiled DNA (light grey) signal was measured at 90 min and normalized to the total signal of the 30 nM WT PRIMPOL reaction. Data are mean ± s.d. from three independent experiments. P values were computed using two-sample two-sided Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests (f and h) and two-tailed two-sided Student’s t-tests (k); NS, not significant (P > 0.05); *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ****P < 0.0001.

To visualize CMG, we used GINS-depleted extract supplemented with fluorescently labelled GINS (GINS–LD655). To monitor DNA synthesis, we supplemented extract with FEN1–KikG (flap endonuclease 1 fused to the fluorescent protein KikG)35. FEN1 is recruited to chromatin through its interaction with PCNA36, and was previously validated as a marker of nascent DNA37, which does not require FEN1’s enzymatic activity37.

In mock-depleted extract, origin firing generated two diverging CMGs travelling at around 300 nucleotides per min with FEN1–KikG signal accumulating behind each helicase (Fig. 1b). To induce RS, the extract was supplemented with 15 µM aphidicolin (APH)—an inhibitor of B-family polymerases (including α, ε and δ) that does not inhibit PRIMPOL (Extended Data Fig. 1d). In APH-treated extract, CMG travelled around 10× slower than in mock without any accompanying FEN1–KikG signal, indicating a failure to synthesize DNA (Fig. 1c). This substantial CMG slowing during RS (reported by us25 and others38) is a hallmark of CMG uncoupling28 (Fig. 1b,c). Adding 30 nM of wild-type (WT) PRIMPOL to APH-treated extract did not support fork restart (Extended Data Fig. 1e), reflecting the fact that APH inhibits Pol ε and δ and prevents them from extending PRIMPOL’s primers.

To recapitulate RS without inhibiting Pol ε/δ, we devised two independent strategies. First, we immunodepleted Pol α from nuclear extract (depleting or inhibiting Pol α was previously used to induce RS in cells22,39,40,41). In Pol-α-depleted extract, CMGs travelled very slowly (around 30 nucleotides per min) without any accompanying FEN1 accumulation (Fig. 1d). This is indicative of helicase uncoupling and is consistent with reports that Pol α is required for establishing leading strand synthesis42,43. When Pol-α-depleted extract was supplemented with recombinant WT PRIMPOL, we routinely observed that slow/uncoupled CMGs suddenly sped up to around 300 nucleotides per min (Fig. 1e (white arrows)). We interpret this switch to fast CMG progression as fork restart. Around 75% of stalled forks restarted in Pol-α-depleted extract supplemented with 30 nM WT PRIMPOL, versus only around 5% restart efficiency in reactions supplemented with buffer (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1f). Importantly, the sudden switch from slow to fast CMG progression was accompanied by FEN1–KikG accumulation behind the fork, indicative of DNA synthesis (Fig. 1e). To corroborate the idea that fast CMG progression corresponds to DNA synthesis, we repeated these experiments with fluorescently labelled PCNA (PCNA–LD655)—an established marker of nascent DNA44,45. Like FEN1–KikG, PCNA–LD655 accumulated behind restarted forks (Extended Data Fig. 1g). Disrupting FEN1’s interaction with PCNA eliminated FEN1–KikG binding (Extended Data Fig. 1h) without impacting fork restart (Extended Data Fig. 1i). We conclude that FEN1–KikG is recruited to nascent DNA by PCNA, and that the sudden speed-up of CMG represents fork restart. We subsequently used FEN1–KikG as a DNA synthesis marker because it provided better signal-to-noise than PCNA–LD655 (Methods).

Second, we designed a DNA substrate with site-specific DNA lesions on the leading strand template, each consisting of a small (around 4 amino acids) peptide adduct (Extended Data Fig. 2a). This lesion should easily fit through CMG’s central channel46, and should induce helicase uncoupling. After encountering the lesion, CMG instantly slowed down from around 300 nucleotides per min to 30 nucleotides per min (Fig. 1g,h), indicative of uncoupling. In the absence of PRIMPOL, forks stalled at the lesion restarted very inefficiently (around 7%) (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1f), probably through TLS as shown previously47,48. In extract containing 30 nM of WT PRIMPOL, around 50% of forks stalled at the lesion restarted (Fig. 1i,f), causing CMG to speed up from around 30 nucleotides per min to 300 nucleotides per min—matching the speed of unperturbed forks (Fig. 1h and Extended Data Fig. 2b). Importantly, lesion-stalled forks restarted in a PRIMPOL-dependent manner in extract containing endogenous levels of Pol α.

We conclude that recombinant human WT PRIMPOL supports robust fork restart in our single-molecule assay using two orthogonal sources of RS (Fig. 1f). We subsequently used the Pol α depletion method because it provided a higher throughput, and was easily adapted for ensemble assays (see below).

To establish an ensemble assay for PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart, we replicated a 3 kb plasmid in Pol-α-depleted extract, which strongly suppressed DNA synthesis in comparison to the mock-depleted extract (Fig. 1j (compare i and ii)). The low levels of DNA synthesis in Pol-α-depleted extract (Fig. 1j (ii)) are probably caused by trace amounts of Pol α that evaded the immunodepletion (Extended Data Fig. 2c).

Supplementing Pol-α-depleted extract with 3–30 nM of WT PRIMPOL led to a significant increase in DNA synthesis, in a PRIMPOL-concentration-dependent manner (Fig. 1j,k). As human cells contain around 17 nM of PRIMPOL49, the concentrations used here are near physiological. Notably, 30 nM of WT PRIMPOL did not fully rescue DNA synthesis (Fig. 1j (v versus i)). We attribute this to the fact that depleting Pol α activates the DNA damage checkpoint (Extended Data Fig. 2c), which partially inhibits origin firing and results in fewer forks (Extended Data Fig. 2d (CDC45 blot)). We revisit CHK1’s role in Fig. 4.

To verify that PRIMPOL is responsible for the partial rescue of DNA synthesis in the biochemical assay, we tested two previously characterized mutants: (1) PRIMPOL D114A/E116A (hereafter, PRIMPOL(AxA)), which lacks primase and polymerase activity2,3; and (2) PRIMPOL D519R/F522A/D551R/I554A (hereafter, PRIMPOL(ΔRPA)), which cannot interact with RPA30 (Extended Data Fig. 1c). The in vitro primase–polymerase assay showed that PRIMPOL(ΔRPA) (but not PRIMPOL(AxA)) exhibits catalytic activity (Extended Data Fig. 1d). Chromatin fractionation experiments indicate that WT PRIMPOL and PRIMPOL(AxA) (but not PRIMPOL(ΔRPA)) are recruited to DNA in Pol-α-depleted extract (Extended Data Fig. 2d) and in APH-treated extract (Extended Data Fig. 2e). In contrast to WT PRIMPOL, neither PRIMPOL(AxA) nor PRIMPOL(ΔRPA) rescued DNA synthesis in Pol-α-depleted extract (Fig. 1j (v–vii)), corroborating reports that repriming requires both PRIMPOL’s enzymatic activity1,4 and its interaction with RPA30,31. These data indicate that Pol-α-depleted extract recapitulates PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart, providing a powerful model system to dissect the molecular mechanism of repriming.

It was previously proposed that RPA recruits PRIMPOL to stalled forks4,30. As uncoupled CMGs generate long tracts of RPA-coated ssDNA, it remained unclear where exactly PRIMPOL binds along ssDNA. To address this question, we visualized AlexaFluor647-labelled WT PRIMPOL (PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647) in Pol-α-depleted extract supplemented with FEN1–KikG, and RPA fused to mCherry-XL50,51 (hereafter, RPA–mCherryXL) (Extended Data Fig. 3a). This enabled us to simultaneously monitor PRIMPOL binding and dissociation, DNA synthesis and the extent of RPA–ssDNA. Importantly, fluorescent labelling did not impair PRIMPOL’s fork restart activity (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c).

At 30 nM of PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647, there were too many PRIMPOL binding events on RPA–ssDNA, making it impossible to resolve individual molecules (Extended Data Fig. 3d). To distinguish each PRIMPOL binding event, we visualized 3 nM PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 at 15 s per frame (Fig. 2a). Initially, RPA–ssDNA tracts grew bidirectionally very slowly (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 3e)—consistent with uncoupled helicases (Fig. 1h). After PRIMPOL-mediated fork restart, RPA–ssDNA tracts grew rapidly, but the RPA signal intensity decreased around twofold (Fig. 2a (bottom)). This suggests that PRIMPOL reprimes synthesis only on one strand (the leading strand, as shown in Fig. 4).

a, Kymogram showing ssDNA coated with RPA–mCherryXL (green) and nascent DNA coated with FEN1–KikG (blue) in Pol-α-depleted extract with 3 nM PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 (magenta). For clarity, the RPA kymogram is shown separately from FEN1 + PRIMPOL. The grey lines mark the boundary of the RPA signal: the dotted lines denote uncoupled CMGs and the dashed lines mark restarted forks. The white arrows indicate fork restart. Bottom inset: integrated RPA signal profile, which decreases by around 50% after fork restart. b, RPA–mCherryXL (green), FEN1–KikG (blue) and PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 (magenta) binding to DNA in Pol-α-depleted extract. The cartoons illustrate the fork status over time. c, Cumulative probability plot of PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 (3 nM) binding event duration, comparing fork-proximal (dark grey) and fork-distal (light grey) binding events in Pol-α-depleted extract (solid lines) or APH-treated extract (dashed lines). n values denote the number of binding events analysed. d, The number of all fork-proximal PRIMPOL binding events per unit time at the fork. e, The number of fork-distal PRIMPOL binding events observed per unit time normalized by the length of exposed ssDNA. In d and e, n values denote the number of forks. Data are mean ± 95% CI, estimated by bootstrapping. f, Cumulative probability plot of fork-proximal (solid lines) and fork-distal (dashed lines) binding events in Pol-α-depleted extract for PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 (dark grey) and PRIMPOL(AxA)–AF647 (orange). n values denote the number of binding events analysed. Data in a–f are from experiments imaged at 15 s per frame. g, Kymograms showing fork restart in Pol-α-depleted extract with 3 nM PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 (magenta) imaged at 3 s per frame. h, Cumulative probability plot of PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 binding event duration in Pol-α-depleted extract imaged at 3 s per frame (at this temporal resolution, short-lived events dominate both fork-distal and fork-proximal subpopulations). n values denote the number of binding events analysed. P values were computed using two-sample two-sided Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests (c–f and h); ***P < 0.001. All experiments were performed twice, with different extract preparations.

We detected numerous short-lived PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 binding events far from replication forks (Fig. 2a (orange triangles)), which we call fork-distal. Most fork-distal PRIMPOL binding events (~84%) lasted one frame (15 s) or less (Fig. 2c) and were randomly distributed along RPA–ssDNA. We also detected fork-proximal PRIMPOL binding events close to the fork (within 1 pixel = 160 nm), which tended to be longer than fork-distal binding events (Fig. 2c). Notably, long-lived fork-proximal PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 binding (Fig. 2a,b (curly brackets)) preceded most (~70 ± 10%) fork restart events (Fig. 2a,b (white arrows)).

To gain further insights, we quantified the frequency of fork-proximal (Fig. 2d) and fork-distal (Fig. 2e) binding events in Pol-α-depleted extract supplemented with 3 nM of fluorescently labelled WT PRIMPOL, PRIMPOL(AxA) or PRIMPOL(ΔRPA). As expected, PRIMPOL(ΔRPA) exhibited very little fork-proximal or fork-distal binding in Pol-α-depleted extract, indistinguishable from the negative control, for which we measured the frequency of non-specific binding using free AF647 dye (Fig. 2d,e and Extended Data Fig. 3f). Both WT PRIMPOL and PRIMPOL(AxA) exhibited high levels of fork-proximal and fork-distal binding in Pol-α-depleted extract, consistent with chromatin fractionation experiments (Extended Data Fig. 2d,e). Notably, PRIMPOL(AxA) exhibited the most fork-proximal binding (Fig. 2d), probably because it can repeatedly bind to stalled forks without restarting them (Extended Data Fig. 3g). By contrast, WT PRIMPOL promotes fork restart, after which it no longer binds to the unstressed fork (the mock-depleted control is shown in Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 3h). Notably, there was no statistical difference between binding event durations for WT PRIMPOL and PRIMPOL(AxA) (Fig. 2f), even though only WT PRIMPOL supported fork restart (Extended Data Fig. 2i).

We also observed long-lived fork-proximal WT PRIMPOL binding events before fork restart on the template with a site-specific lesion (Extended Data Fig. 3j). These productive WT PRIMPOL binding events lasted around 3 min, similar to those measured in Pol-α-depleted extract (Extended Data Fig. 3j). Notably, there was a delay of 3–5 min between the dissociation of PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 from the fork, and fork restart (Extended Data Fig. 3j). This delay probably reflects the time needed for a replicative polymerase to capture the primer synthesized by PRIMPOL, and for the reassembly of an active replisome.

Occasionally, we observed PRIMPOL binding in consecutive movie frames at nearby positions on DNA (Fig. 2b (light blue ovals)). This could represent a PRIMPOL molecule diffusing along ssDNA, or may represent different molecules binding at slightly different positions along ssDNA. To distinguish between these scenarios, we repeated the experiment at 3 s per frame (Fig. 2g, five times faster than in Fig. 2a–f). At this higher frame rate, we frequently observed different PRIMPOL molecules briefly binding to ssDNA in non-consecutive video frames (Fig. 2g (white ovals)). Such binding sequences could be misinterpreted as diffusion of a single PRIMPOL molecule if imaged at lower framerates. This experiment also revealed that the vast majority of PRIMPOL binding events are very short-lived, lasting 3 s or less (Fig. 2h). We still observed long-lived fork-proximal binding events that preceded fork restart (Fig. 2g (white curly brackets)). In summary, although we cannot rule out PRIMPOL diffusion across short distances, our data argue against long-range PRIMPOL diffusion on ssDNA.

Although PRIMPOL can transiently bind anywhere along ssDNA–RPA (Fig. 2a,b), the vast majority (over 99%) of binding events are non-productive—that is, they do not lead to fork restart. Productive PRIMPOL binding events occur predominantly near stalled forks and tend to be long-lived (~3 min; Extended Data Fig. 3j), raising the question of why fork-proximal binding events are longer. We hypothesized that PRIMPOL’s binding at the fork may be stabilized by yet unknown interactions with fork-associated proteins. Notably, AlphaFold3 predicted that several replisome subunits may interact with PRIMPOL52. By cross-referencing AlphaFold predictions for human and frog proteins, we singled out PRIMPOL’s putative interaction with MCM4—a CMG subunit (Fig. 3a). Positively charged residues in human PRIMPOL (Arg29, Arg31, Lys34) are predicted to form salt bridges with MCM4 residues (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). To test this prediction, we generated three mutants: PRIMPOL R29A/R31A/K34A (hereafter, PRIMPOL(3A)), PRIMPOL R29D/R31E/K34D (hereafter, PRIMPOL(DED)) and PRIMPOL(29–35:Linker) (in which residues 29–35 were replaced with the linker GGGSGGGS) (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 4c,d).

a, View of the predicted interaction between human PRIMPOL residues 28–40 (pink) and Xenopus MCM4 residues 466–479 and 670–689 (green) (left). Right, the PRIMPOL–MCM4 model superimposed onto the cryo-EM structure of the core human replisome (PDB: 7PFO). b, PRIMPOL mutants designed to disrupt the interaction with MCM4. c, The cumulative probability distribution of fork-proximal binding events for PRIMPOL constructs shown in b. n values denote the total number of binding events. d, Representative western blot image from a co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) experiment in which Flag–SNAP–PRIMPOL(1–60) constructs were immobilized on anti-Flag beads and incubated with Xenopus extract. e, Quantification of the co-IP experiment shown in d from three independent repeats. Data are mean ± s.d. f, Representative autoradiogram of the replication assay in mock-depleted or Pol-α-depleted extract with 30 nM WT PRIMPOL, 30 nM PRIMPOL(3A), 30 nM PRIMPOL(DED) or 30 nM PRIMPOL(29–35:Linker). Repl., replicated. g, Quantification of replication assay shown in f from three independent repeats. Total DNA synthesis (dark grey) and supercoiled plasmid (light grey) signal was measured at 90 min and normalized to the total signal of the WT PRIMPOL control. Data are mean ± s.d. from three independent experiments. h, Diagram of the DNA fibre fork restart assay. PRIMPOL-knockout (KO) cells were transfected with plasmids encoding WT PRIMPOL, PRIMPOL(3A), PRIMPOL(DED) or PRIMPOL(29–35:Linker). Forks were pulse-labelled with CldU (red), irradiated with UV-C, allowed to recover and then pulse-labelled with IdU (green). Representative fibre tracks show a fork that restarted and a fork that did not. i, Quantification of fork restart efficiency measured in DNA fibre experiments (the number of restarted forks divided by the total number of forks). Data are mean ± s.d. from four independent experiments (WT, KO, KO + WT) or three independent experiments (KO + 3A, KO + DED, KO + 29-35:Linker). P values were computed using two-sample two-sided Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests (c) and two-tailed two-sided Student’s t-tests (e, g and i).

First, we measured the duration of fork-proximal PRIMPOL binding events in APH-treated extract. APH does not alter the duration of PRIMPOL-binding events (Fig. 2c) but allows PRIMPOL to repeatedly bind without promoting fork restart (Extended Data Fig. 4e). All three PRIMPOL mutants exhibited significantly reduced fork-proximal binding times compared with WT PRIMPOL (Fig. 3c), suggesting that disrupting the predicted PRIMPOL–MCM4 impairs PRIMPOL recruitment to stalled forks.

Second, we co-immunoprecipitated MCM2–7 from extract using PRIMPOL residues 1–60 as bait. We compared the WT bait versus the 3A, DED and 29-35:linker mutants (Extended Data Fig. 4f). All three mutant bait proteins co-immunoprecipitated with MCM2–7 less efficiently than the WT PRIMPOL(1–60) bait (Fig. 3d,e), corroborating AlphaFold’s prediction.

Third, we examined whether the three full-length PRIMPOL mutants can reprime stalled forks in Pol-α-depleted extract. PRIMPOL(DED) and PRIMPOL(29–35:Linker) mutants exhibited significant defects in DNA synthesis while PRIMPOL(3A) showed a more subtle defect (Fig. 3f,g). Notably, all three mutants exhibited similar enzymatic activity in vitro (Extended Data Fig. 4d), consistent with the fact that residues 29–35 are in a disordered region distant from the catalytic core. Notably, AlphaFold3 predicted that PRIMPOL may also interact with MCM753, which is located next to MCM4 within CMG (Extended Data Fig. 4b). These additional interactions with MCM7 may explain the modest defect of PRIMPOL(3A) in the biochemical fork restart assay (Fig. 3f,g). To disrupt PRIMPOL’s interaction with both MCM4 and MCM7, we prepared the mutant PRIMPOL K8E/E13R/R15E/R29D/R31E/K34D (PRIMPOL(EREDED)). Unfortunately, PRIMPOL(EREDED) exhibited diminished enzymatic activity in vitro (Extended Data Fig. 4d), so we did not investigate it further.

Finally, we examined whether the PRIMPOL–MCM4 interaction is important for fork restart in human cells, using an established DNA fibre assay1 (Fig. 3h). Plasmids encoding WT or mutant PRIMPOL were transiently transfected into PRIMPOL-deficient HCT116 cells. Both PRIMPOL(DED) and PRIMPOL(3A) mutants were expressed at levels similar to WT PRIMPOL, while PRIMPOL(29–35:Linker) was expressed at lower levels that were similar to endogenous PRIMPOL (Extended Data Fig. 4g). To measure the fork-restart efficiency, ongoing forks were pulse-labelled with 5-chloro-2′-deoxyuridine (CldU) for 20 min and cells were irradiated with UV-C light (30 J m−2) to arrest fork progression. Cells were allowed to recover for 30 min and were pulse-labelled with 5-iodo-2′-deoxyuridine (IdU) for 20 min to label only forks that restarted (Fig. 3h). DNA fibre analysis revealed that the PRIMPOL(DED) and PRIMPOL(29–35:Linker) mutants significantly impaired fork restart compared with the WT control (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 4h). While the PRIMPOL(3A) mutant also impaired fork restart, it exhibited more variability between experimental repeats, rendering the difference between WT PRIMPOL and PRIMPOL(3A) not statistically significant (Fig. 3i). The findings presented in Fig. 3 indicate that the PRIMPOL–MCM4 interaction helps target PRIMPOL to stalled forks, and is required for efficient fork restart.

We found that WT PRIMPOL promotes efficient fork restart at concentrations as low as 3 nM (Fig. 2a,b). In the low PRIMPOL concentration regime, restart involves long-lived PRIMPOL binding to the fork through MCM4. Consequently, we refer to these events as CMG-dependent restart. Notably, at higher concentrations of WT PRIMPOL (>10 nM), we observed a distinct subpopulation of restart events that occurred far behind the fork (Fig. 4a (white asterisks)). The frequency of these fork-distal restart events increased proportionally to WT PRIMPOL concentration (Fig. 4b (grey bars)), indicating that they also represent repriming.

a, Kymogram showing a bidirectional replication bubble undergoing fork restart in Pol-α-depleted extract with 30 nM unlabelled WT PRIMPOL. RPA–mCherryXL (green) and FEN1–KikG (blue) are shown overlaid or separately. The white arrows indicate CMG-dependent fork restart. The white asterisks indicate CMG-independent restart events. Both types of restart event cause RPA clearing from a parental DNA strand. b, CMG-dependent (green) and CMG-independent (grey) restart efficiency in Pol-α-depleted extract supplemented with buffer, or various concentrations of WT PRIMPOL or PRIMPOL(DED). c, DNA synthesis rates measured in Pol-α-depleted extract supplemented with 30 nM of unlabelled WT PRIMPOL or PRIMPOL(DED) extracted from RPA tract growth (before and after CMG-dependent restart) or from FEN1 tract growth (after CMG-independent (indep.) restart). The blue lines indicate the median values and the shaded boxes represent the 95% CI estimated by bootstrapping. n values denote the number of restart events. d, Fork restart efficiency measured in Pol-α- and mock-depleted extract; Pol-α- and Pol-δ-depleted extract; and Pol-α- and Pol-ε-depleted extract. The reactions were supplemented with 30 nM of unlabelled WT PRIMPOL and 400 nM Pol δ or 100 nM Pol ε. e, The fork restart efficiency measured in Pol-α-depleted extract supplemented with 30 nM of unlabelled WT PRIMPOL or PRIMPOL phosphomutants (PRIMPOL(Δ201–260), PRIMPOL(S255E), PRIMPOL(S255D), PRIMPOL(S255A)). f, The fork restart efficiency measured in Pol-α-depleted extract supplemented with increasing concentrations of WT PRIMPOL or PRIMPOL(Δ201–260). For b–f, data are mean ± 95% CI, estimated by bootstrapping, n values denote the number of forks. P values were computed using two-sample two-sided Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests. All experiments were performed twice with different extract preparations.

We repeated experiments with PRIMPOL(DED) and observed a substantial decrease in CMG-dependent restarts (Fig. 4b (green bars)), but not in fork-distal restarts (Fig. 4b (grey bars) and Extended Data Fig. 5a,b). This suggests that the latter represent a distinct type of restart event, which we call CMG independent. Notably, the FEN1-labelled nascent DNA tracts grew significantly faster during CMG-independent restart (~700 nucleotides per min) than during CMG-dependent restart (~300 nucleotides per min) (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 5c), corroborating our hypothesis that CMG-dependent and CMG-independent restarts are mechanistically distinct (see below).

We conclude that PRIMPOL supports two distinct types of restart event: (1) CMG-dependent restart that requires the PRIMPOL–CMG interaction and is efficient at limiting PRIMPOL concentrations; and (2) CMG-independent restart that does not require the PRIMPOL–CMG interaction and becomes efficient only at high PRIMPOL concentrations that mimic overexpression15.

The PRIMPOL–CMG interaction raises the possibility that PRIMPOL’s primer could be handed directly to the leading strand polymerase Pol ε, which is physically tethered to CMG54,55,56 in a manner that should not prevent PRIMPOL from binding to MCM4 (Fig. 3a). If so, Pol ε could capture PRIMPOL’s primer and extend it to restart leading strand synthesis. Alternatively, PRIMPOL’s primer could be extended by Pol δ first, and then handed to Pol ε, reminiscent of how leading strand synthesis is established during replication initiation42,57.

To test these hypotheses, we performed experiments in extract depleted of Pol α and Pol δ, or in extract depleted of Pol α and Pol ε (Fig. 4d). Depleting Pol δ caused only a minor reduction in CMG-dependent fork restart efficiency, whereas depleting Pol ε ablated CMG-dependent restart events (Fig. 4d (green bars) and Extended Data Fig. 6a–c). Importantly, CMG-dependent fork restart was fully rescued by adding 100 nM (Pol ε concentration in human cells49) of recombinant Pol ε to Pol-ε-depleted extract (Fig. 4d and Extended Data Fig. 6d). These data support the hypothesis that CMG-dependent restart entails the primer handover from PRIMPOL to Pol ε, which subsequently performs long-range DNA synthesis.

Notably, depleting Pol δ (but not Pol ε) eliminated CMG-independent restart events (Fig. 4d (grey bars) and Extended Data Fig. 6a). Supplementing Pol-δ-depleted extract with 400 nM (Pol δ concentration in human cells)49 of recombinant Pol δ fully rescued CMG-independent restart (Fig. 4d and Extended Data Fig. 6e,f). These findings suggest that CMG-independent restart entails the primer handover from PRIMPOL to Pol δ, which subsequently performs long-range DNA synthesis.

We conclude that PRIMPOL primarily acts as a leading-strand primase by synthesizing primers immediately behind CMG, and those primers are extended by Pol ε. However, at higher concentrations, PRIMPOL can also reprime DNA synthesis in a CMG-independent manner, and those primers are extended by Pol δ. Our observation that DNA synthesis proceeds faster during CMG-independent restart (Fig. 4c) may reflect the fact that this process does not require template unwinding, or may point to Pol δ being able to synthesize DNA faster than Pol ε.

It was previously reported that CHK1 phosphorylates human PRIMPOL at Ser255, which promotes more repriming and RS tolerance in human cells22. The same study proposed that a disordered loop in human PRIMPOL (residues 201–260) autoinhibits repriming, but that Ser255 phosphorylation by CHK1 relieves this autoinhibition22. We examined whether CHK1 modulates PRIMPOL’s activity in our biochemical fork restart assay. We supplemented Pol-α-depleted extract with an ATR inhibitor (AZD6738) that blocked CHK1 phosphorylation (Extended Data Fig. 7a (lane iii versus iv)). Notably, inhibiting ATR in Pol-α-depleted extract enhanced the amount of PRIMPOL-dependent DNA synthesis (Extended Data Fig. 7b (v versus vi) and 7c). This indicates that checkpoint activation is not required for PRIMPOL to restart stalled forks. This finding also explains the low levels of DNA synthesis reported in Fig. 1j: depleting Pol α activates the DNA damage checkpoint, which suppresses origin firing, resulting in fewer replication forks (Extended Data Fig. 2d (CDC45 immunoblot)). Thus, although PRIMPOL can restart most stalled forks in Pol-α-depleted extract, the overall amount of DNA synthesis is expected to be lower than in the mock control (Fig. 1j (i versus v)).

Immunoblotting of phosphorylated CHK1 in Pol-α-depleted extract collected from the flow cell revealed that the checkpoint is not active in our single-molecule experiments. This is because the DNA template concentration in the flow-cell is very low (10−3−10−2 ng μl−1) while checkpoint activation requires at least around 1 ng μl−1 (ref. 58) of DNA template. The fact that we observe robust PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart in the single-molecule assay (Fig. 1f) in the absence of CHK1 activation (Extended Data Fig. 7a (flow-cell lane)) supports our conclusion that checkpoint activation is not required for repriming.

Given the report that CHK1 stimulates PRIMPOL activity in human cells22, we hypothesized that CHK1 may regulate another aspect of PRIMPOL’s function. To test this idea, we performed single-molecule fork restart experiments with four previously characterized PRIMPOL phospho-mutants22 (Extended Data Fig. 7d,e): phospho-dead PRIMPOL(S255A), phosphomimetic PRIMPOL(S255E) and PRIMPOL(S255D), and a mutant that phenocopies the phosphomimetic mutants—PRIMPOL(Δ201–260) (in which residues 201–260 were replaced by a flexible linker). At a near-physiological concentration (30 nM), all four mutants supported similar levels (80–90%) of CMG-dependent fork restart to WT PRIMPOL (Fig. 4e (green bars) and Extended Data Fig. 7f). However, the mutants supported different levels of CMG-independent restart (Fig. 4e (grey bars)): PRIMPOL WT and PRIMPOL(S255A) exhibited the lowest efficiency (~25%); PRIMPOL(S255E) and PRIMPOL(S255D) supported intermediate efficiency (~40%); while PRIMPOL(Δ201–260) displayed the highest efficiency (~70%).

We further examined PRIMPOL(Δ201–260) across a wide range of concentrations (Fig. 4f). At near-physiological concentrations (10 nM and 30 nM), PRIMPOL(Δ201–260) supported significantly more CMG-independent restart than WT PRIMPOL (Fig. 4f (grey bars) and Extended Data Fig. 7g). We conclude that CHK1 phosphorylation of Ser255 does not affect PRIMPOL’s primary mode of repriming (CMG dependent), but significantly enhances PRIMPOL’s secondary repriming mode (CMG independent). Consistent with our conclusion, the stimulatory effect of CHK1 phosphorylation on PRIMPOL’s activity was previously observed in cells treated with a Pol α inhibitor22—which exposes large tracts of ssDNA behind the fork, generating the ideal substrate for CMG-independent repriming.

Our experiments revealed several mechanistic insights into PRIMPOL function, dynamics and regulation, supporting a new model of PRIMPOL-mediated fork restart (Fig. 5). First, PRIMPOL can briefly bind anywhere along RPA–ssDNA (Fig. 5a–c), but such binding events are very short-lived (Fig. 5c) and rarely cause fork restart. Second, PRIMPOL can reside on RPA–ssDNA much longer near uncoupled CMGs (Fig. 5d–f), and such long-lived binding events frequently lead to fork restart. Third, the PRIMPOL–MCM4 interaction is required for efficient fork restart (Fig. 5e) in nuclear extract and in human cells. Finally, our data indicate that, at near-physiological concentrations, PRIMPOL primarily acts as a leading-strand primase, and that PRIMPOL’s primers are directly handed to Pol ε (Fig. 5f–h). Notably, PRIMPOL-driven restart can also occur far behind stalled forks (Fig. 5i–l), but only at high PRIMPOL concentrations (mimicking overexpression), or after ATR/CHK1 activation. It is tempting to speculate that chemotherapy-induced PRIMPOL overexpression observed in cancer cells14,15 may unlock this alternative CMG-independent restart mechanism. As PRIMPOL cannot prime on ssDNA fully coated with RPA30, CMG-independent repriming events may occur only when a RPA molecule transiently dissociates from ssDNA in PRIMPOL’s immediate vicinity (Fig. 5i,j). Notably, RPA can spontaneously dissociate from ssDNA in vitro59, albeit slowly (koff = 0.006 s−1).

a, During unperturbed replication, Pol ε and Pol δ synthesize the leading and lagging strands, respectively, minimizing the accumulation of RPA-coated ssDNA. b, During RS, CMG becomes uncoupled from DNA synthesis and continues to unwind DNA, generating RPA-coated ssDNA. c, PRIMPOL transiently binds to RPA far from CMG, but such fork-distal binding events are short-lived and rarely lead to repriming. d, PRIMPOL binds to RPA near CMG. e, PRIMPOL simultaneously interacts with both RPA and MCM4, which prolongs PRIMPOL’s residence at the stalled fork. f, Long-lived fork-proximal binding enables PRIMPOL to synthesize a short primer behind CMG. g, After PRIMPOL dissociates, Pol ε captures the primer synthesized by PRIMPOL. h, Pol ε elongates the primer and restarts leading-strand synthesis. i, At high PRIMPOL concentrations, there are many short-lived PRIMPOL binding events on RPA–ssDNA. j, Infrequent RPA dissociation generates exposed ssDNA near PRIMPOL. k, PRIMPOL synthesizes a primer far behind CMG. l, Pol δ captures the primer synthesized by PRIMPOL and elongates it, restarting DNA synthesis independently of CMG. b–h, (blue-shaded panels) CMG-dependent fork restart is efficient at low PRIMPOL concentrations and occurs independently of CHK1 signalling. i–l, (red-shaded panels) CMG-independent fork restart becomes more frequent at higher PRIMPOL concentrations (which mimic overexpression) and depends on CHK1 phosphorylation of PRIMPOL at Ser255.

We show that efficient repriming requires both PRIMPOL–RPA and PRIMPOL–MCM4 interactions. As RPA binds to PRIMPOL’s C terminus30 and MCM4 binds to PRIMPOL’s N terminus (Fig. 3), we propose that PRIMPOL simultaneously interacts with both RPA and MCM4 during repriming (Fig. 5e). This model provides simple-yet-elegant answers to three long-standing questions. First, PRIMPOL can interact with both RPA and MCM4 only behind uncoupled CMGs, explaining how PRIMPOL is targeted specifically to stalled forks (Fig. 5e). Second, the simultaneous interaction with both RPA and MCM4 positions PRIMPOL near CMG’s exit channel (Fig. 3a). This enables PRIMPOL to engage the leading-strand template before it is coated by RPA (Fig. 5f), explaining how repriming can occur in the nucleus where RPA is very abundant. Third, PRIMPOL’s binding to CMG facilitates rapid primer handover to Pol ε (Fig. 5g), minimizing error-prone DNA synthesis during repriming. It is unclear what causes PRIMPOL’s dissociation after primer synthesis but before fork restart (Fig. 2b). It is possible that PRIMPOL disengages RPA once the primer becomes too long (Fig. 5f), which could promote PRIMPOL’s dissociation from DNA. Alternatively, PRIMPOL may transiently dissociate from MCM4 while CMG recruits replication factors that prevent PRIMPOL from re-binding the helicase.

Notably, we observed a negligible amount of PRIMPOL binding to unperturbed forks (mock in Fig. 2d,e and Extended Data Fig. 3h). This could be because, during normal replication, there is no RPA-coated ssDNA immediately behind CMG (Fig. 5a). Alternatively, during unperturbed replication, PRIMPOL’s docking site on CMG may be sterically occluded by a replication elongation factor. For example, CTF18 binds to the C terminus of MCM7 (ref. 45) (next to MCM4), which may prevent PRIMPOL binding to CMG during replication elongation.

During the preparation of this manuscript, we became aware of a similar study60 from the Yeeles group (MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge, UK), which reconstituted PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart using purified human proteins and obtained a cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of the CMG–PRIMPOL complex that is highly similar to the AlphaFold prediction (personal communication).

There are a few notable similarities between PRIMPOL’s role in the nucleus and mitochondria. First, PRIMPOL interacts with the mitochondrial replicative helicase Twinkle61 and the ssDNA-binding protein mtSSB9, reminiscent of its interactions with CMG and RPA. Notably, PRIMPOL also interacts with the mitochondrial DNA polymerase γ61, but there is no evidence of PRIMPOL interacting with Pol ε/δ. Second, PRIMPOL is required to restart replication after mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) damage61, similar to its role in restarting forks in the nucleus. Notably, Twinkle can stimulate PRIMPOL’s enzymatic activity in vitro62, but it remains unclear how this regulates repriming in mitochondria. Third, PRIMPOL overexpression leads to increased levels of lagging strand priming during mtDNA replication, reminiscent of CMG-independent restart events observed by us at high PRIMPOL concentrations (Fig. 4b (grey bars)). The ability of PRIMPOL to restart DNA synthesis far behind CMG may reflect a vestigial or primordial role of PRIMPOL to prime mtDNA lagging strand synthesis. This activity is normally suppressed by ssDNA-binding proteins (RPA or mtSSB), but becomes possible after PRIMPOL overexpression. Notably, DNA damage checkpoint activation and the subsequent phosphorylation of PRIMPOL by CHK1 (ref. 22) further upregulate CMG-independent repriming (Fig. 4e,f).

Although PRIMPOL is regarded as an attractive therapeutic target17,63, currently there are no small-molecule PRIMPOL inhibitors. Our findings suggest an alternative strategy to inhibit repriming—namely, to prevent PRIMPOL binding to CMG. This could be accomplished using peptides or molecules that bind to PRIMPOL’s N terminus, which normally interacts with MCM4–CMG.

Eggs from adult laboratory-bred female X. laevis frogs (Xenopus 1, 4800) were used to prepare egg extracts. Testes from adult laboratory-bred male X. laevis frogs (Xenopus 1, 4293) were used to prepare sperm chromatin. All animals were healthy, 2–3 years of age, not subjected to previous procedures and no animal husbandry was performed. No animal randomization or blinding was performed. Frogs were housed at the Boswell Small Amphibians Research Facility at Stanford School of Medicine and all experiments involving frogs were approved by Stanford’s Institute Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC-33670).

PRIMPOL-proficient and PRIMPOL-KO HCT116 cells were generated in the Méndez laboratory and cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (Sigma-Aldrich, D5796) supplemented with 10% FBS (Biowest S1810) plus 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Solmeglas, L0018). All human cell lines were routinely tested for mycoplasma contamination and consistently tested negative throughout the course of the study.

Sf9 cells (Expression Systems, 94-001S) and Tni cells (Expression Systems, 94-002S) were cultured in ESF 921 insect cell culture medium (Expression Systems, 96-001-01) at 27 °C for baculovirus production and protein overexpression.

DH10EMBacY (Geneva Biotech, DH10EMBacY), DH5α (New England Biorabs (NEB), C2987H) and Rosetta (DE3) pLysS (Novagen, 70956-4) bacteria were cultured in TB (RPI Research Products, T15050) or LB broth (Thermo Fisher Scientific, BP9723) at 37 °C for plasmid production and protein overexpression.

In vitro transcription and translation (IVTT) reactions were performed using the TnT SP6 High-Yield Wheat Germ Protein Expression System (Promega, L3261) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Proteins were not purified after production by IVTT.

X. laevis egg extracts were prepared according to published protocols64,65. Frogs were primed with 50 IU of human chorionic gonadotropin (CHORULON) (Merck, 133754) 5 days before extract preparation. To induce ovulation, 500 IU of CHORULON was injected 21–22 h before extract preparation. Sperm chromatin was purified from adult male frog testes and used for nucleoplasmic extract (NPE) preparation.

To prepare antigens consisting of X. laevis PRIMPOL amino acids 1–212, X. laevis POLA1 amino acids 1–340, POLD1 amino acids 1–89, POLE1 amino acids 578–754 and full-length X. laevis PCNA, the corresponding DNA sequence was PCR amplified out of X. laevis egg cDNA. The resulting PCR product was assembled into pET28b(+) using the NEBuilder HiFi Mix (NEB, E2621S), yielding plasmids pJP001 (PRIMPOL), pGC279 (POLA1), pLDL048 (POLD1), pLDL037 (POLE1) and pLDL190 (PCNA).

To prepare human WT His6-SNAP-PRIMPOL, synthetic gene blocks were ordered from Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT) and assembled into pET28b(+) using the NEBuilder HiFi Mix (NEB, E2621S), yielding plasmid pJP012.
